one: A VM emulates a whole computer with its own OS kernel. A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel.
an: A VM is a separate house with its own foundation and plumbing. Containers are apartments in one building: private rooms, shared foundation and pipes.
how: A hypervisor (KVM, Hyper-V, ESXi) runs VMs. Each VM boots its own guest kernel and OS. Strong isolation, but a normal cloud VM takes tens of seconds to boot and carries a full OS in memory and on disk.

A container is a normal Linux process wrapped in kernel features: namespaces (it sees its own filesystem, process list, network, hostname) and cgroups (limits on CPU, memory, process count). It usually starts in well under a second, because nothing has to boot.

On macOS, Docker Desktop runs a small Linux VM and your containers run inside it, because Linux containers need a Linux kernel. On Windows it uses WSL 2 (also a lightweight VM) for Linux containers; native Windows containers exist but are rare in web work.

MicroVMs such as Firecracker sit in between: a VM with a tiny device model that boots in a fraction of a second. AWS Lambda and Fargate use Firecracker to get VM-level isolation with near-container speed.
why: Containers made it cheap to package an app with its exact dependencies and run dozens per machine. That density is what made modern orchestration practical.
trade: Weaker isolation than VMs because the kernel is shared, so a kernel exploit can escape. Cloud providers run your containers inside VMs (or micro-VMs like Firecracker) for that reason.

myth.m: A container is a lightweight VM.
myth.r: It is a process with blinders on. The image contains OS files (for example Debian's libc and shell), but there is no second kernel. Every container on a host shares the host kernel, which is why uname -r inside a container prints the host's kernel version.

q.s: Why do containers start in milliseconds while VMs take far longer?
o: Containers use SSDs
A container is just a process on an already-running kernel; a VM boots an entire OS
Containers skip networking
VMs are written in Java
q.e: No boot sequence. The kernel is already up.

cgroups v2 for CPU and memory limits

Run docker run --memory=50m with a program that allocates 200MB and watch it get killed.
On a Linux VM, try unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc sh to create a namespace by hand.

plain:
A virtual machine pretends to be a whole separate computer, with its own operating system. A container is just a normal program on a shared operating system, but wearing blinders: it sees only its own files, its own processes and its own network.

That is why containers start in a fraction of a second and are small, while VMs take longer and are heavier.
bridge: Docker Desktop on your Mac actually runs a small Linux VM in the background, and your containers run inside it, because containers need a Linux kernel.

walk.title: Running Postgres two ways
steps: VM way: create a virtual machine, boot Ubuntu (a minute), install Postgres, configure it. The VM uses gigabytes of disk and memory for a full OS.
Container way: docker run -p 5432:5432 postgres:16. It starts in about a second.
Inside the container, ps shows only Postgres. It cannot see your other programs.
It uses your machine's existing (Linux) kernel, so there is no second operating system to boot.
Delete the container and it is gone, unless you stored data in a volume.

terms: A fully emulated computer with its own OS.
An isolated process sharing the host's OS kernel.
The core of the operating system that manages hardware and processes.
insights: Pick the tool by who wrote the code. Your own trusted services: containers are fine. Code from strangers (user scripts, CI jobs from forks): VMs, microVMs or gVisor.
“Serverless containers” (Fargate, Cloud Run, Lambda) still run inside microVMs or sandboxes. You just do not manage them.
Container start time is mostly image pull plus your app's own boot. The container itself adds almost nothing, so a slow start is usually a big image or a slow app.

prod.summary: In production, containers almost always run inside VMs: the cloud gives you VMs (nodes), and you pack many containers onto each. Seniors care about two things here: isolation (a shared kernel means one kernel bug can affect every container on the node) and resource limits (a container without cgroup limits can starve its neighbours).
checklist: Every container has a memory limit and a CPU limit or request; nothing runs unlimited on a shared node.
Untrusted or multi-tenant code (user scripts, CI jobs from forks) runs in a stronger sandbox: separate VMs, Firecracker microVMs, or gVisor, not plain containers.
Containers run as a non-root user and drop Linux capabilities they do not need; --privileged is never used for app workloads.
The container runtime (runc, containerd) and host kernel are patched; container escapes are usually runtime or kernel bugs.
The app reads its limits from cgroups, not from the host: thread pools and heap sizes are set for the container's CPU and memory, not the node's.
No state lives only in the container's writable layer; data goes to volumes or managed services.
numbers: Firecracker microVMs boot in as little as about 125 ms (Firecracker project docs).
Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). For a container this usually means the kernel OOM killer hit the cgroup memory limit, or a stop timeout ran out.

runc CVE-2024-21626 (“Leaky Vessels”, January 2024) allowed a container escape through a leaked file descriptor; fixed in runc 1.1.12. A reminder that the shared kernel/runtime is the isolation boundary.
With cgroups v2, a container's memory limit is visible at /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max and its CPU quota at /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max.
failures: Inside a container limited to 512 MB, free -m shows 64 GB, and a JVM or cache sized itself to “available memory” gets OOMKilled.

/proc/meminfo shows the host's memory; the limit is enforced by cgroups. Size heaps and caches from the cgroup limit (/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max; Node: --max-old-space-size; modern JVMs read cgroups automatically) and leave headroom.
A Go or Java service on a 64-core node with a 2-CPU limit shows terrible p99 latency and high CPU throttling (nr_throttled climbing in /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat).

The runtime saw 64 CPUs and started 64 worker threads, which burn the 2-CPU quota early in each 100 ms period and then wait. Go 1.25+ sets GOMAXPROCS from the cgroup CPU limit (it ignores the CPU request), and JDK 10+ is container-aware. If you run without a CPU limit, Go still sees all 64 CPUs, so set GOMAXPROCS yourself, for example from the request via the downward API.
Security review flags that a CI system runs pull-request builds from external contributors in Docker containers on shared hosts.
A shared kernel is not a strong boundary for hostile code. Run untrusted jobs in throwaway VMs or microVMs (Firecracker, Kata) or a gVisor sandbox.
File-watching dev server inside Docker Desktop on a Mac is slow and misses changes.
Bind mounts cross the boundary between macOS and the Linux VM. Use VirtioFS file sharing, keep heavy folders like node_modules in a container volume, or use Compose watch mode.

code.title: A container is a process with cgroup limits, not a VM
code.src:
# Start a container with a 256 MB memory cap and half a CPU
docker run -d --name demo --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 node:22-slim sleep infinity

# Same kernel as the host: no second OS booted
uname -r
docker exec demo uname -r

# The limits are cgroup v2 files
docker exec demo cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max   # 268435456
docker exec demo cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max      # 50000 100000

# But /proc still shows the host's memory
docker exec demo sh -c 'grep MemTotal /proc/meminfo'

# From the host, the container is just a process
docker top demo

# After a crash, check whether the OOM killer did it
docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' demo
code.note: cpu.max of 50000 100000 means 50 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, which is half a CPU. The MemTotal line is why apps that size themselves from /proc get killed.

qs.s: You are building a platform where customers upload and run their own code. Which isolation choice is the reasonable production default?
o: Plain Docker containers with --memory and --cpus limits
Containers running as a non-root user, otherwise default settings
A microVM (Firecracker, Kata) or gVisor sandbox per customer workload
One large VM with all customers in separate folders
qs.e: Hostile code needs a boundary stronger than a shared kernel. Limits and non-root are good hygiene, but a single kernel or runtime bug still lets code escape. MicroVMs give each workload its own kernel at near-container speed; this is what AWS Lambda and Fargate do.

qs.s: A container started with --memory=512m runs free -m and sees 64 GB total memory. What is going on?
o: free reads /proc/meminfo, which shows the host's memory; the 512 MB limit is enforced by cgroups and shown in /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max
Docker failed to apply the limit, so the container can use all 64 GB
The container has its own kernel, configured with 64 GB
The limit only takes effect after the container restarts
qs.e: The limit is real: the kernel will OOM-kill the process at 512 MB. But /proc is not virtualised per container, so tools and runtimes that read it see the host. That mismatch is a classic cause of OOMKilled containers.

qs.s: Your image is based on ubuntu:24.04. The host is Amazon Linux running kernel 6.12. What does uname -r print inside the container?
o: Ubuntu 24.04's default kernel version
Nothing: containers do not have a kernel
A special Docker kernel version
6.12, the host's kernel version
qs.e: The image only provides Ubuntu's user-space files. All containers share the host kernel, so uname reports the host. This is also why a container cannot use a kernel feature the host kernel lacks.

qs.s: A Go 1.25 payment service runs on a 64-core node. The team expected Go's container-aware GOMAXPROCS to match the pod's 2 CPUs, but the log says 64. Read the output. Why?

code.title: kubectl output
code.src:
$ kubectl get pod pay-7c9 -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'
{"requests":{"cpu":"2","memory":"1Gi"},"limits":{"memory":"1Gi"}}

$ kubectl exec pay-7c9 -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max
max 100000

$ kubectl logs pay-7c9 | head -1
go1.25.1 starting, GOMAXPROCS=64

o: Go reads the cgroup CPU limit, not the request. There is no CPU limit (cpu.max is max), so Go uses all 64 node CPUs; set GOMAXPROCS explicitly
Container-aware GOMAXPROCS is off by default and must be enabled with a GODEBUG flag
Kubernetes hides cgroup files from containers, so Go cannot read any limit
Go reads the CPU request, but only after the first garbage collection
qs.e: The Go 1.25 release notes say the runtime uses the cgroup CPU bandwidth limit and “does not consider the CPU requests option”. cpu.max = max means no quota, so there is nothing lower than 64. The GODEBUG option is tempting, but it works the other way: containermaxprocs=0 turns the feature off; it is on by default. Fix: set GOMAXPROCS=2 as an env var, or set it from requests.cpu with a downward API resourceFieldRef.

qs.s: This Node service runs in Kubernetes with a 512 MiB memory limit on a 64 GiB node. It caches responses until the cache reaches its budget. What happens under steady traffic?

code.title: cache.ts

o: It works: inside a container os.totalmem() returns the cgroup limit
Node refuses to start because the budget is larger than the limit
os.totalmem() reports the node's 64 GiB, so the budget is about 16 GiB; the cache grows past 512 MiB and the kernel OOM-kills the container (exit 137)
Kubernetes moves the extra memory to swap, so the service just gets slower
qs.e: Like free, os.totalmem() reports host memory, not the cgroup limit. The cache never hits its 16 GiB budget before the 512 MiB limit, so the container is OOMKilled again and again. Read the real limit from /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max or pass the budget as config. Kubernetes nodes usually run without swap, and even where swap is enabled, the memory limit still applies.

qs.s: On a Mac, Docker Desktop's Linux VM is set to 4 GB of memory. You run docker run --memory=8g for a data job that needs 6 GB. What happens?
o: The container gets 8 GB, because limits come from macOS
The container can never use more than the Linux VM's memory (about 4 GB, minus what the VM itself uses), so the job is OOM-killed; raise the VM's memory in Docker Desktop settings
Docker on macOS ignores --memory completely
macOS swaps memory for the container, so 8 GB works exactly like on a Linux server
qs.e: On a Mac, containers run inside a Linux VM. The cgroup limit of 8 GB is only a ceiling; the real memory available is what the VM has. The job hits the VM's limit and the Linux OOM killer stops it. This is the same reason a container on a 4 GB cloud VM cannot use 8 GB, whatever its limit says.

qs.s: A node has 16 vCPU and 64 GiB. After system reservations, 15 vCPU and 60 GiB are allocatable. Each pod requests 500m CPU and 3Gi memory. How many of these pods can the scheduler place on the node?
o: 16, one per vCPU
20, because memory runs out first: 60 / 3 = 20
qs.e: The scheduler checks every resource. CPU would allow 30 pods, but memory allows only 20, so memory is the binding limit. 32 uses the raw node size and ignores reservations. This is why right-sizing memory requests often matters more than CPU for density.

interview.q: We let customers run their own code on our platform. Would you run it in containers or VMs? Explain the trade-off.
answer: Containers share the host kernel. Namespaces and cgroups limit what a process sees and uses, but one kernel or runtime bug (for example runc CVE-2024-21626) can let hostile code escape to the host and to other tenants.
VMs have their own kernel behind a hypervisor, a much smaller attack surface, but are slower to start and use more memory.
The middle path is microVMs (Firecracker, Kata) or a user-space kernel like gVisor: VM-level isolation with near-container start times. AWS Lambda uses Firecracker for exactly this case.
Defence in depth still applies: non-root, dropped capabilities, seccomp, read-only root filesystem, no host mounts, network egress rules, and strict CPU, memory and PID limits.
Decision: trusted internal services in containers on shared nodes; untrusted tenant code in a microVM or sandbox per tenant or per job.
followups: What does gVisor cost you compared with plain runc?
How would you stop one tenant from starving others on the same node?

interview.q: A service in Kubernetes has low average CPU, but p99 latency is bad and Grafana shows CPU throttling. Walk me through what is happening.
answer: A CPU limit becomes a CFS quota in cpu.max, for example 50000 100000 = 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period. A burst that uses the quota early waits for the rest of the period, which adds up to tens of ms to a request.
Averages hide this: 30% average use can still mean many throttled periods. Check nr_throttled and throttled_usec in cpu.stat, or container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total in Prometheus.
Runtimes that size thread pools from the host CPU count make it worse (many threads share a small quota). Go 1.25+ and JDK 10+ read the limit; Node's libuv pool and others need explicit settings.

Fixes: raise or remove the CPU limit and keep an honest request (many teams run latency-sensitive services without CPU limits), set runtime thread counts to match, and scale out with an HPA if real usage is high.
Trade-off: no CPU limit means a noisy pod can take spare CPU from neighbours; requests still guarantee each pod its share under contention.
followups: How would you prove throttling is the cause and not GC or the database?
When would you keep CPU limits anyway?

interview.q: Why do cloud providers usually run your containers inside VMs? Would you ever run containers on bare metal?
answer: The VM is the security and billing boundary between customers. Containers from different customers should not share a kernel.
VMs also make capacity elastic: nodes are created and destroyed through an API, and node failure is handled by replacing the VM.
Inside one company's trust boundary, bare-metal nodes remove hypervisor overhead and give direct hardware access (GPUs, NVMe, NICs). Large platforms do run Kubernetes on bare metal.
The cost is slower provisioning, harder isolation between teams, and doing your own hardware lifecycle (firmware, disks, replacement).
Rule of thumb: bare metal when you have steady, large, trusted workloads and an ops team; VMs for everything else.
followups: How does Fargate or Cloud Run isolate customers?
What changes for noisy-neighbour problems on bare metal?

one: Docker builds images (a frozen filesystem + startup command) and runs them as containers (live instances of an image).
an: An image is a recipe card that also contains the pre-measured ingredients. A container is one dish cooked from it. You can cook 50 identical dishes from one card.
how: A Dockerfile lists steps: FROM node:22-slim, WORKDIR /app, COPY package.json package-lock.json ./, RUN npm ci, COPY . ., CMD ["node", "server.js"]. When COPY has several sources, the destination must be a directory ending in /.
Each step creates a cached layer. If package.json and the lockfile did not change, the npm ci layer is reused, which is why you copy dependency files before source code.
Multi-stage builds compile in a big image and copy only the output into a small runtime image. Images are pushed to a registry (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR) and pulled wherever they run.
Containers are ephemeral: anything written inside is lost when the container is replaced. Persistent data goes to volumes or external services.

Use the exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"]. With the shell form CMD node server.js, Docker runs /bin/sh -c "node server.js". Some shells replace themselves with node, others stay as PID 1 and do not pass SIGTERM on — so whether your app hears docker stop depends on the base image. CMD npm start has the same risk. Exec form removes the guesswork.
why: "Works on my machine" disappears: the image you tested is byte-for-byte the image that runs in production.
trade: Images bloat (1GB+ with dev dependencies), leak secrets if you COPY .env, and run as root by default. Use slim bases, .dockerignore, multi-stage builds and a non-root user.

myth.r: Docker is tooling around Linux containers. On Linux there is no VM at all.

q.s: Every code change makes the Docker build reinstall all npm packages (4 minutes). Likely Dockerfile mistake?
o: Using node:22
COPY . . comes before RUN npm ci, so any source change invalidates the install layer
Not using Kubernetes
Missing CMD
q.e: Copy package.json and the lockfile first, install, then copy the rest. Source edits then reuse the cached install layer.

more: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD, and exec form vs shell form (signals!)
Multi-platform builds (arm64 vs amd64, relevant on Apple Silicon)
lab: Write a Dockerfile for a Node API: copy lockfile first, npm ci, then source; non-root user; .dockerignore.
Convert it to a multi-stage build and compare image sizes with docker images.
Run docker history on the image and find the biggest layers.
Send docker stop and confirm your app receives SIGTERM and shuts down cleanly (log it).

plain:
Docker packages your app with everything it needs (the right Node version, system libraries, your code, your dependencies) into an image. Running an image creates a container.

The same image runs the same way on your laptop, in CI and in production. That removes the “works on my machine” problem.
bridge: An image is like the output of npm run build, but it also includes the runtime and the operating system files. You build it once and run it anywhere.

walk.title: Packaging a Node API
steps: FROM node:22-slim: start from an image that already has Node.
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ then RUN npm ci: install dependencies. Docker caches this layer.
COPY . .: add your source code. Code changes only rebuild from here, so builds stay fast.
USER node and CMD ["node", "server.js"]: run as a non-root user, start the app.
docker build -t api:1.0 . then docker run -p 3000:3000 api:1.0. Push the image to a registry and production pulls the exact same thing.

terms: A frozen package: filesystem + settings + start command.
A running instance of an image.
The recipe for building an image.
One cached step of the build; unchanged layers are reused.
Storage that survives when the container is removed.
insights: The image is the release, not the Dockerfile. Build once in CI and promote the same image; rebuilding per environment can pull a newer base image and ship different bytes.
Keep runtime config out of the image. The same image should run in dev, staging and production with only env vars and mounted files changing.
docker history on an image you did not build shows its build steps. It is a quick way to find bloat and leaked secrets.

prod.summary: In production the image is the deployable unit: CI builds it once, tags it with the commit SHA, and every environment runs that exact image. Seniors review Dockerfiles for four things: cache order (build speed), size and attack surface (slim or distroless base, multi-stage), secrets (never baked into layers), and shutdown behaviour (exec-form CMD, SIGTERM handling, non-root user).
checklist: Lockfile is copied and npm ci runs before COPY . ., so code changes reuse the dependency layer.
Multi-stage build: dev dependencies, compilers and source maps stay in the build stage; the runtime stage has only production deps and build output.
A .dockerignore excludes .git, node_modules, .env and test fixtures.
Runs as a non-root user (USER node), with a pinned base image tag (node:22.x-slim or a digest), not node:latest.
Secrets are passed with RUN --mount=type=secret at build time or as env/files at run time, never with ARG, ENV or COPY .env.
CMD uses exec form, and the app handles SIGTERM: stop accepting requests, finish in-flight ones, close DB pools, exit.
The image is built for the platform it runs on (--platform linux/amd64, or a multi-arch build) when developers use Apple Silicon.
numbers: docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits 10 seconds by default, then sends SIGKILL (exit code 137).

Exit code 143 = 128 + 15: the process was ended by SIGTERM without handling it. Exception: a process running as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM unless it installs a handler, so Node as PID 1 with no handler is not stopped by SIGTERM at all and ends with 137 after the timeout. Use a handler or --init.
Docker docs warn that build ARG values are visible in docker history and in provenance attestations, so they are not safe for secrets.
Deleting files in a later RUN step does not make the image smaller: each layer is stored, and the later layer only hides the files.
failures: Every docker stop or deploy takes exactly 10 seconds per container, and the app never logs “shutting down”.
Shell-form CMD or npm start means sh or npm is PID 1 and the signal never reaches Node. Use exec form CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"], add a SIGTERM handler, or run with --init (tini).
Image works on a developer's M-series Mac, but on the x86 server the container exits at once with exec format error.
The image was built for arm64. Build with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 (or linux/amd64,linux/arm64 for multi-arch) in CI, not on laptops.
Security scan finds an npm token in a public image, even though the Dockerfile deletes .npmrc after install.

The file or the ARG value was recorded in an earlier layer or in the image history. Rotate the token, then use RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci, which never writes it to a layer.
Image is 1.4 GB and pulls take a minute on every new node, slowing autoscaling.
Full node:22 base plus dev deps and build tools. Switch to a slim or distroless runtime stage, npm ci --omit=dev, and check docker history for the biggest layers.
Container restarts lose uploaded files and SQLite data.
Data was written to the container's writable layer. Mount a volume, or better, use object storage and a managed database.

code.title: Multi-stage Node image: cached deps, non-root, exec form
code.src:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:22-slim AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist
COPY --chown=node:node package.json ./
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
code.note: The runtime stage never sees dev dependencies or source. CMD in exec form makes Node PID 1 so it receives SIGTERM; the app still needs a process.on("SIGTERM") handler to drain requests.

qs.s: Every deploy waits exactly 10 seconds per container to stop, and the app never logs its “shutting down” message. The Dockerfile ends with CMD npm start. What is the most likely cause?
o: The image is too large to stop quickly
The healthcheck keeps failing during shutdown
Docker always waits 10 seconds before stopping any container
npm (run via a shell) is PID 1 and does not pass SIGTERM to Node, so Docker gives up after 10 s and sends SIGKILL
qs.e: Docker sends SIGTERM and waits 10 s by default. If the signal never reaches Node, nothing shuts down cleanly and the container is killed. Use exec form with node directly, handle SIGTERM, or add --init. Docker does not always wait the full 10 s: a container that exits on SIGTERM stops immediately.

qs.s: A developer builds on an M3 MacBook and pushes. On the x86 production server the container exits instantly with exec format error. Why?
o: The image got corrupted during push
The image was built for arm64, and the x86 server cannot run those binaries
The CMD uses shell form instead of exec form
The entrypoint script is missing chmod +x
qs.e: exec format error means the CPU cannot execute the binary format. Build with --platform linux/amd64 or a multi-arch build in CI. A missing execute bit gives permission denied, not this error.

qs.s: A Dockerfile has ARG NPM_TOKEN and RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc && npm ci && rm .npmrc. Is the token safe if the image is pushed?
o: No: build args are recorded in the image history and provenance; use RUN --mount=type=secret instead
Yes: the file is deleted in the same RUN, so no layer contains it
Only unsafe if the registry is public
Yes: ARG values are never stored anywhere in the image
qs.e: Deleting the file in the same step does keep it out of the layer, which is why “the file is deleted in the same RUN” is tempting. But the ARG value itself is visible via docker history. Private registries leak too (former employees, CI logs). Secret mounts never touch the image.

qs.s: A developer on a Mac builds this image. The repository has no .dockerignore. The container crashes at start with the error in the comment. What is the cause?

code.title: Dockerfile
code.src:
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# docker run api:dev
# Error: /app/node_modules/bcrypt/lib/binding/napi-v3/bcrypt_lib.node:
#   invalid ELF header

o: bcrypt does not support Node 22
npm ci failed silently, so bcrypt was never installed
The slim image lacks build tools, so bcrypt could not compile
COPY . . copied the Mac's own node_modules over the Linux one, so the native module is a macOS binary; add node_modules to .dockerignore
qs.e: “invalid ELF header” means Linux tried to load a file that is not a Linux binary: here a Mach-O file built on macOS. npm ci did install the right Linux build, but the later COPY . . replaced it. Missing build tools would fail during npm ci at build time, not at run time. A .dockerignore also speeds up builds and keeps .env and .git out.

qs.s: The team added a cleanup step to shrink the image, but it is still about 900 MB. Read the history. Why did the cleanup not help?

code.title: docker history api:3f9a2c1 (trimmed)
code.src:
SIZE      CREATED BY
0B        CMD ["node" "dist/server.js"]
1.1kB     RUN apt-get purge -y build-essential python3 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
6.3MB     RUN npm run build
412MB     RUN npm ci
2.4MB     COPY . .
301MB     RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential python3
190MB     FROM node:22-slim

o: apt-get purge does not delete files, it only marks packages as removed
Layers are additive: the 301 MB layer is still in the image, and the purge layer only hides those files; use a multi-stage build so build tools never reach the runtime image
The purge must run before npm ci to work
Docker compresses layers, so the size shown is wrong and the real image is small
qs.e: Every RUN creates a layer that is stored and pulled. Removing files later adds a small layer that marks them deleted; the bytes stay. Either install, use and remove the tools in one RUN, or better, build in one stage and copy only dist and production node_modules into a clean runtime stage. Compression lowers transfer size, but the stored layers still contain the tools.

qs.s: Given this Dockerfile, what process does docker run img worker.js start?

code.title: Dockerfile
code.src:
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
ENTRYPOINT ["node"]
CMD ["server.js"]

o: node worker.js: arguments after the image name replace CMD, and ENTRYPOINT stays
worker.js alone, which fails because it is not executable
node server.js worker.js
Docker exits with an error because CMD and run arguments conflict
qs.e: With exec-form ENTRYPOINT, CMD provides only default arguments. Run-time arguments replace CMD and are appended to the entrypoint. To replace the entrypoint itself you need --entrypoint. In Kubernetes, command overrides ENTRYPOINT and args overrides CMD.

qs.s: You move the runtime stage to a distroless Node image and add HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:3000/healthz || exit 1. The app serves traffic fine, but docker ps shows it as unhealthy. Why?
o: The app crashes between health checks
Docker ignores HEALTHCHECK in multi-stage builds
Distroless images have no shell and no curl, so the check command cannot run and counts as a failure; use an exec-form check with Node, for example ["/nodejs/bin/node", "healthcheck.js"]
Port 3000 is not in an EXPOSE line, so the check cannot reach it
qs.e: Shell-form HEALTHCHECK runs under /bin/sh -c, and distroless has neither sh nor curl. EXPOSE is only documentation; the check runs inside the container and can reach any local port. Note that Kubernetes ignores Docker HEALTHCHECK completely and uses its own probes.

interview.q: Walk me through how you would write and review a production Dockerfile for a TypeScript Node service.
answer: Multi-stage: a build stage with dev dependencies compiles TypeScript; a runtime stage gets only dist and production node_modules (npm ci --omit=dev).
Cache order: copy package.json and the lockfile, run npm ci, then copy source. Use BuildKit cache mounts for the npm cache.
Small, pinned base (node:22-slim with a version, or a digest; distroless if the team can debug without a shell); a .dockerignore for .git, node_modules, .env.
Security: USER node, no secrets in ARG/ENV/layers (use RUN --mount=type=secret), image scanned in CI.
Runtime behaviour: exec-form CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] so Node gets SIGTERM, a SIGTERM handler that drains, and memory settings that fit the container limit.
Built in CI for the target platform (multi-arch if needed), tagged with the git SHA.
followups: Why not run npm start as the CMD?
Slim vs distroless vs Alpine: what would you pick and why?

interview.q: Our image is 1.4 GB and the build takes 8 minutes on every commit. How would you fix both?
answer: Measure first: docker history or dive to find the big layers, and the build log to see which steps miss the cache.
Size: multi-stage build, slim or distroless runtime base, --omit=dev, no build tools or source maps in the final stage, delete caches in the same RUN that creates them.
Speed: dependency files before source, BuildKit cache mounts (--mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm), and a shared CI cache (--cache-from/--cache-to to a registry).
A .dockerignore shrinks the build context; sending .git and node_modules to the builder alone can cost a lot of time.
Why it matters: image size affects pull time on every new node, so it slows autoscaling and recovery, not only CI.
followups: How does BuildKit's registry cache work in CI runners that start empty?
When does Alpine (musl) cause problems for Node?

interview.q: How does a container shut down, and how do you make deploys lose zero requests?
answer: The runtime sends SIGTERM to PID 1, waits a grace period (10 s in Docker, 30 s by default in Kubernetes), then sends SIGKILL.
PID 1 is special: it gets no default signal handling, so it must handle SIGTERM itself. Shell-form CMD or npm start puts a shell or npm in front of the app; use exec form or --init (tini).
On SIGTERM the app stops accepting new connections (server.close()), finishes in-flight requests, closes idle keep-alive connections, closes DB pools, then exits.
In Kubernetes, endpoint removal happens in parallel with SIGTERM, so a short preStop sleep keeps the pod serving while load balancers update.
Grace period must cover preStop plus the longest request; otherwise SIGKILL cuts requests. Verify by running a load test during a rollout and counting 5xx.
followups: What exit code would you expect after a clean shutdown?
How do long-lived WebSocket connections change the plan?

package-lock.json"] B --> C["RUN npm ci"] C --> D["COPY . ."] D --> E["USER node + CMD"] E --> F["Image api:1.0"] F -->|docker push| R[(Registry)] F -->|docker run| K1[Container 1] F -->|docker run| K2[Container 2]

diagrams.title: docker stop: why exec form matters
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as docker stop
  participant S as sh or npm
  participant N as node server.js
  alt Shell form or npm start: sh or npm is PID 1
    D->>S: SIGTERM
    Note over S,N: Signal is not passed on to Node
    D->>S: SIGKILL after 10 s
    Note over N: Killed mid-request, exit 137
  else Exec form: Node is PID 1
    D->>N: SIGTERM
    N->>N: Handler drains requests, closes DB pool
    N-->>D: Exits 0 in under 10 s
  end
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the signal goes to PID 1 only. With CMD ["node", "server.js"] Node gets SIGTERM and can shut down cleanly. Node still needs a process.on("SIGTERM") handler, because as PID 1 it ignores SIGTERM without one.

one: A YAML file that defines several containers (app, Postgres, Redis) and starts them together with one command.
an: A seating plan for a dinner party: who comes, where they sit, who talks to whom. docker compose up seats everyone.
how: compose.yaml lists services, their images or build context, ports, environment variables, volumes and dependencies. docker compose up -d creates or updates them; it recreates only services whose config or image changed.

Compose creates a private network per project. Services reach each other by service name as a hostname: the app connects to db:5432, not localhost. Published ports: are only for reaching a service from the host or the outside.

Start order: short-form depends_on waits only for the container to start. Use condition: service_healthy (with a healthcheck) to wait for readiness, or condition: service_completed_successfully to wait for a one-off job such as migrations.
Data: named volumes survive down and are deleted by down -v. Bind mounts map a host folder into the container, which is useful for live code editing in development.
Variables like ${DB_PASSWORD} come from the shell or an .env file next to the compose file. ${DB_PASSWORD:?must be set} stops with an error instead of silently using an empty value.
Great for local development, CI test stacks and simple single-server deployments; it does not spread containers across machines.
why: A new teammate runs one command and has the whole stack, at the same versions as everyone else.
trade: Compose runs on one machine. It does not do self-healing across machines, rolling deploys at scale or autoscaling. That is the job orchestrators like Kubernetes take on.

myth.r: Compose is for one host and development. Kubernetes is for clusters. Many teams use Compose locally and Kubernetes (or a PaaS) in production.

q.s: Inside the app container, connecting to localhost:5432 fails, though Postgres is in the same compose file. Why?
o: Postgres is down
localhost is the app container itself; use the service name, e.g. postgres:5432
Wrong password
Compose does not support Postgres
q.e: Each container has its own network namespace. Compose provides DNS by service name.

more: Override files for dev vs CI
lab: Write a compose.yaml with app + Postgres + Redis. Use a named volume for Postgres data.
Add a Postgres healthcheck so the app waits for it.
Run docker compose down then up and confirm data survived; then down -v and confirm it did not.

plain:
Real apps need several containers: your app, a database, maybe Redis. Docker Compose describes all of them in one YAML file and starts them together with one command.

Inside that setup, containers find each other by their service name, like a hostname.
bridge: It is the npm run dev for your whole backend: one command and a new teammate has the app, Postgres and Redis running with the right versions.

walk.title: A full local stack in one file
steps: compose.yaml lists three services: app (built from your Dockerfile), db (postgres:16), cache (redis:7).
The app's env var is DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/app. Note the host is db, the service name, not localhost.
The db service has a named volume so data survives restarts, and a healthcheck.
depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy makes the app wait until Postgres is ready.
docker compose up starts everything; docker compose down stops it; down -v also deletes the data.

terms: One container definition in a compose file.
Docker-managed storage that persists between runs.
A command Docker runs to know if a container is ready.
Compose puts services on a private network where names resolve to containers.
insights: Inside a container, “localhost” means that container itself, not your laptop or another container.
depends_on only orders the first start. Later, services restart on their own, so the app must survive the database going away and coming back.
A good compose.yaml is also documentation: a new teammate sees every service, port, env var and dependency of the backend in one file.

prod.summary: Compose is the standard way to run a local stack and is fine for small single-server production. Seniors check readiness (does the app wait for a healthy database?), data safety (named volumes, backups), and network exposure (what ports are open to the internet). On a single server there is no failover: if the host dies, everything dies.
checklist: Databases have a healthcheck, and the app uses depends_on: condition: service_healthy; the app also retries its DB connection on its own.
Database data lives in a named volume, and there is a real backup (pg_dump to off-host storage), because a volume is not a backup.
Internal services (Postgres, Redis) have no ports: entry, or bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
Secrets come from an .env file that is not committed, or from Compose secrets:; compose.yaml holds no passwords.
Images use pinned tags (postgres:16.4, not postgres:latest) so a restart does not silently upgrade a database.
Long-running services have restart: unless-stopped and log rotation configured, so a full disk does not take the host down.
numbers: Docker healthcheck defaults: interval 30s, timeout 30s, retries 3, start_period 0s. With defaults, an unhealthy service needs about 90 seconds to be marked unhealthy.
The top-level version: key is obsolete in the Compose Specification; current Compose ignores it and prints a warning.
docker compose down keeps named volumes; docker compose down -v deletes them, with no confirmation.
failures: On a fresh docker compose up the app crashes with ECONNREFUSED db:5432; on the second try it works.

Short-form depends_on: [db] waits only for the container to start, not for Postgres to accept connections. Add a pg_isready healthcheck and condition: service_healthy, and add connection retries in the app.
A port scan finds Postgres open on the public IP, although ufw denies port 5432.
ports: ["5432:5432"] binds to 0.0.0.0, and Docker writes its own iptables rules that bypass ufw. Remove the port mapping or use "127.0.0.1:5432:5432".
After editing DATABASE_URL in compose.yaml and running docker compose restart app, the app still uses the old value.
restart restarts the existing container and does not apply config changes. Run docker compose up -d, which recreates changed services.
The whole local database is empty after a teammate's cleanup script.
The script ran docker compose down -v, which deletes named volumes. Keep seed scripts, and never use -v on hosts with real data.
The server's disk fills up after a few weeks and all containers stop.
The default json-file log driver has no size limit unless configured. Set logging: options: max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" or configure the daemon's log options.

code.title: compose.yaml: app waits for a healthy Postgres, DB not exposed
code.src:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:${DB_PASSWORD}@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  pgdata:
code.note: The app connects to host db, the service name. Binding Postgres to 127.0.0.1 keeps it reachable from your laptop's tools but not from the internet. ${DB_PASSWORD} comes from an uncommitted .env file.

qs.s: On the first docker compose up, the app crashes with ECONNREFUSED db:5432. Running it again works. The app has depends_on: [db]. Best fix?
o: Add a healthcheck to db and use depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy, plus connection retries in the app
Change the host from db to localhost
Change the port mapping to "5433:5432"
Add the old links: key so the containers can see each other
qs.e: Short-form depends_on only orders container start. Postgres needs a few seconds before it accepts connections. The host name db is already correct; localhost would point at the app container itself.

qs.s: Your VPS runs Compose with Postgres mapped as "5432:5432". ufw denies 5432, yet an external scan finds Postgres open. Why?
o: ufw rules need a reboot to apply
Postgres opens the port by itself using UPnP
Docker adds its own iptables rules for published ports, which bypass ufw; bind to 127.0.0.1 or remove the mapping
Compose networks are public by default
qs.e: This is a well-known Docker behaviour on Linux. Published ports go through Docker's iptables chains before ufw's rules. Containers on the same Compose network do not need any published port to talk to each other.

qs.s: You change an environment variable in compose.yaml and run docker compose restart app. The app still sees the old value. What should you run?
o: docker compose build --no-cache app
docker compose up -d, because restart does not apply changes from compose.yaml
Nothing: env vars only change after a host reboot
docker compose down -v then up
qs.e: restart restarts the existing container with its old config. up -d sees the config changed and recreates the container. Rebuilding is not needed for env changes, and down -v would also delete your database volume.

qs.s: There is no .env file on the new CI runner. docker compose up prints The "DB_PASSWORD" variable is not set. Defaulting to a blank string. and starts everything. The db container exits at once with Error: Database is uninitialized and superuser password is not specified, and the app cannot connect. How do you make this fail fast and clearly next time?

code.title: compose.yaml
code.src:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:${DB_PASSWORD}@db:5432/app
  db:
    image: postgres:16.4
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}

o: Use ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme} so there is always a value
Use ${DB_PASSWORD:?DB_PASSWORD is not set}, so Compose refuses to start and prints that message
Move the password into the Dockerfile with ENV
Add restart: always so the app retries until the password is right
qs.e: An unset variable becomes an empty string with only a warning. The :? form turns it into a hard error before any container starts. A default like changeme hides the problem and puts a weak password in use. ENV in a Dockerfile bakes the secret into the image.

qs.s: For live reload, a developer mounts the project into the container. The repository has no node_modules on the host (they only use Docker). The app crashes with Error: Cannot find module 'express', although the image ran npm ci. Why?

code.title: compose.yaml
code.src:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    command: npm run dev
    working_dir: /app
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

o: npm ci does not install express in development
working_dir must be set in the Dockerfile, not in Compose
The port mapping blocks module loading
The bind mount .:/app covers the image's /app, including /app/node_modules; add an anonymous volume - /app/node_modules or use Compose watch
qs.e: A mount replaces what the image had at that path. The host folder has no node_modules, so the container sees none. An extra volume at /app/node_modules keeps the image's (Linux-built) modules visible. Compose develop.watch avoids the problem by syncing files instead of mounting the whole folder.

qs.s: You try docker compose up -d --scale api=3 with this file. What happens?

code.title: compose.yaml
code.src:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports:
      - "80:80"

o: Three replicas start, and Compose load-balances port 3000 across them
Compose ignores --scale unless you use Swarm
The first replica binds host port 3000; the others fail with port is already allocated. Remove the host port and let the proxy reach api:3000 on the network
All three start, but only one receives traffic
qs.e: One host port can be bound once. Scaled services should not publish a fixed host port. Inside the Compose network, the name api resolves to all replicas, so a proxy in front can reach them. Compose itself does not load-balance published ports.

qs.s: A one-off migrate service runs database migrations and exits. The app service must start only after migrations finished successfully. Which depends_on condition do you use on app?
o: migrate: { condition: service_completed_successfully }
migrate: { condition: service_healthy }
migrate: { condition: service_started }
No condition; add restart: always to migrate instead
qs.e: service_completed_successfully waits until the container exits with code 0, which is what a migration job does. service_healthy is tempting, but a container that exits is never “healthy”, so the app would never start. restart: always would rerun migrations forever.

interview.q: When would you run production on Docker Compose, and when would you move off it?
answer: Compose on one server is fine for internal tools, early products and low-traffic apps where some downtime during host failure or reboot is acceptable.
What you give up: no failover across machines, no rolling deploys by default (up -d recreates containers, so there is a short gap), no autoscaling, and manual host patching.

If you stay: managed database instead of a Postgres container, off-host backups, a reverse proxy with TLS, pinned image tags, log rotation, restart: unless-stopped, ports bound to 127.0.0.1 except the proxy.
Move off when uptime needs exceed one host, traffic needs more than one machine, or deploys must have zero downtime. The next step is often a PaaS or ECS/Cloud Run, not straight to Kubernetes.
Compose files still help after the move: they stay the local dev and CI test environment.
followups: How would you get zero-downtime deploys on a single Compose host?
Where should the database live in this setup?

interview.q: Design the local development environment for a team of ten using Compose. What goes in it?
answer: App services built from the same Dockerfile as production (a dev target in a multi-stage build), plus Postgres, Redis and any queue at the same major versions as production.
Healthchecks with service_healthy, and a migration/seed service with service_completed_successfully, so docker compose up works on the first try.
Live reload with Compose watch or bind mounts that keep node_modules in the container; VirtioFS on Macs.
Profiles for optional heavy services (--profile observability), and an override file for personal tweaks that is not committed.
Secrets from an uncommitted .env with a committed .env.example; ${VAR:?} for required values.
The same file runs integration tests in CI, so “works locally” and “works in CI” mean the same thing.
followups: How do you keep the dev database in sync with production schema changes?
How do you handle Apple Silicon vs x86 images?

interview.q: In CI, the app sometimes cannot connect to the database at startup, and a rerun fixes it. How do you debug and fix it?
answer: Classic race: the app starts before Postgres accepts connections. Check whether depends_on is short-form, which waits only for container start.
Add a real readiness healthcheck (pg_isready -U app -d app) with a short interval and enough retries, and use condition: service_healthy.
Also make the app retry its first connection with backoff. Production databases restart and fail over too; startup must not depend on order.
Read docker compose logs db and docker inspect health output to see how long Postgres takes on the CI machine; slow CI disks make init scripts take longer.
If migrations run at start, separate them into their own service so a slow migration is not mistaken for a broken database.
followups: Why can pg_isready succeed while the app still fails?
How would you make the test stack start faster?

one: A storage service for container images, versioned by tags and content digests.
an: npm, but for whole runnable images instead of packages.
how: CI builds an image and pushes it: ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2. Servers and clusters pull it to run.

Tags are movable labels (latest or even 1.4.2 can be re-pushed to point at new content). Digests (@sha256:...) are immutable content addresses: same digest, same bytes. Some registries (ECR, Harbor, Artifact Registry) can make tags immutable.

Some registries scan images for known vulnerabilities themselves (ECR, Artifact Registry, Harbor with Trivy, Docker Hub with Docker Scout). GHCR does not scan images by itself, so teams run Trivy or Grype in CI. Signing is done by a tool such as cosign in CI; the registry stores the signature next to the image, and the cluster can verify it before running.
A multi-arch image is an index: one tag and digest that points at one image per platform (amd64, arm64). Each node pulls the variant for its own CPU.
why: It is the hand-off point between "built" and "deployed". Promoting the same digest from staging to production guarantees you ship exactly what you tested.
trade: Deploying :latest makes rollbacks and audits guesswork. Pin versions or digests.

myth.m: Tagging latest is fine since we always want the newest.
myth.r: Two nodes pulling latest minutes apart can run different code. Rollback has nothing to roll back to.

q.s: Production broke after a deploy, and nobody can tell which image is running because everything is tagged latest. Prevention?
o: Tag images with the git SHA or a version, deploy by that tag or digest
Use a bigger registry
Never deploy
Rebuild in production
q.e: Immutable, traceable versions make "what is running" and "roll back to what" answerable.

more: Image digests and pinning by digest
Retention policies to delete old images
Pull rate limits on Docker Hub
lab: Build an image, tag it with your git SHA, push it to GitHub Container Registry.
Pull it by digest (@sha256:...).
Scan it with trivy image and read the findings.

plain:
A container registry stores your images, like npm stores packages. Your CI builds an image and pushes it there; your servers pull it from there to run it.

Each image has a tag (a readable label like 1.4.2) and a digest (a fingerprint of the exact contents that can never change).
bridge: It is npm publish and npm install, but for whole runnable apps. GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io) works with the GitHub account you already have.

walk.title: From commit to running image
steps: You merge to main. CI builds the image and tags it with the git commit SHA: ghcr.io/you/api:3f9a2c1.
CI pushes it to the registry.
The deploy step tells production to run api:3f9a2c1.
Something breaks. You know exactly which commit is running and roll back to api:8be41d0, the previous one.
If you had only used :latest, you would not know what was running or what to roll back to.

terms: A server that stores and serves images.
A movable human-readable label on an image.
A content hash (sha256:...) that identifies exact image contents.
Download from / upload to a registry.
insights: A tag answers “which commit?”; a digest answers “which exact bytes?”. Use both: the SHA tag for humans, the digest for deploys.
The registry is on the critical path of scale-out. If it is down or rate-limited, running pods are fine but new pods cannot start.
Base images age even when your code does not. Rebuild regularly so OS security fixes reach production.

prod.summary: The registry is the hand-off between CI and runtime, so it is on the critical path of every deploy and every autoscaling event. Seniors make tags traceable (git SHA), deploy or promote by digest, keep rollback images from being deleted, and remove the dependency on Docker Hub rate limits by mirroring base images into their own registry.
checklist: Images are tagged with the git SHA (and optionally a semver), and tags are immutable in the registry settings (ECR and Harbor support this).
Staging and production run the same digest; production is never a rebuild of the same commit.
Retention policies delete old untagged images but keep at least the last N releases so rollback works.
Nodes and CI pull with credentials, and third-party base images are mirrored or pulled through a cache, not straight from Docker Hub.
CI fails the build on new critical CVEs, and images are signed (cosign) and verified at admission where policy requires it.
Multi-arch manifests are pushed if the fleet has both amd64 and arm64 nodes (for example Graviton).
numbers: Docker Hub pull limits: 100 pulls per 6 hours per IPv4 address (or IPv6 /64) for unauthenticated users, 200 per 6 hours for authenticated Personal accounts (Docker docs). Hitting it returns toomanyrequests.
In Kubernetes, imagePullPolicy defaults to Always when the tag is :latest or missing, and to IfNotPresent for any other tag.
A digest is sha256: plus 64 hex characters; it changes if any byte of the image manifest changes.
failures: Autoscaling adds nodes, and new pods sit in ImagePullBackOff with toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit.
All nodes share one NAT IP and pull anonymously from Docker Hub. Authenticate pulls, or mirror base and third-party images into ECR/GHCR/Artifact Registry and reference them there.
After a hotfix re-pushed api:1.4, some pods run the new code and some the old.
Nodes that already had api:1.4 cached did not re-pull (IfNotPresent). Never reuse tags; deploy a new SHA tag or pin by digest. Enable tag immutability so it cannot happen again.
Rollback fails with manifest unknown / not found for the previous version.
A retention rule deleted it (for example “keep last 10 images” while CI pushes many branch builds). Keep release tags in a separate repository or exclude them from cleanup.
ImagePullBackOff with no match for platform in manifest on new arm64 nodes.
The image was pushed for amd64 only. Build multi-arch with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push.

code.title: CI: tag by git SHA, push, record the digest
code.src:
set -euo pipefail
IMAGE=ghcr.io/acme/api
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD)

echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u "$GHCR_USER" --password-stdin

# Multi-arch build, pushed straight to the registry
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t "$IMAGE:$SHA" \
  --push .

# The immutable reference to deploy and promote
DIGEST=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE:$SHA" --format '{{json .Manifest.Digest}}' | tr -d '"')
echo "deploy: $IMAGE@$DIGEST"

# Production later runs exactly this, never a rebuild:
# image: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:...
code.note: The SHA tag tells humans which commit is running; the digest guarantees which bytes are running. Promote the digest from staging to production.

qs.s: A hotfix was built and re-pushed as api:1.4 (same tag). After kubectl rollout restart, some pods run the fix and some still run old code. Why?
o: The registry needs time to replicate the new image
For non-latest tags, imagePullPolicy defaults to IfNotPresent, so nodes that cached api:1.4 did not pull again
Kubernetes stores the image itself in etcd
The Service is still routing to terminated pods
qs.e: Same tag, different bytes, and each node decides for itself. Never reuse a tag: push a new SHA tag or deploy by digest, and turn on tag immutability in the registry.

qs.s: Your cluster's nodes all leave through one NAT IP and pull anonymously from Docker Hub. A traffic spike adds 30 nodes, and each new node pulls 4 Docker Hub images. What happens?
o: Nothing: the limit is counted per node
Nothing: the images are already cached in Docker Hub's CDN
All pulls fail, because Docker Hub blocks Kubernetes clusters
About 120 pulls from one IP exceed the 100-per-6-hours anonymous limit, so some pods get toomanyrequests and ImagePullBackOff
qs.e: 30 × 4 = 120 pulls from a single IP, above the unauthenticated limit of 100 per 6 hours. It hits exactly when you need capacity most. Authenticate, or mirror the images into your own registry.

qs.s: Staging tested image api@sha256:ab12… built from commit 3f9a2c1. For production, a teammate proposes rebuilding from the same commit “to be safe”. What do you say?
o: Agree: a fresh build picks up the newest security patches
Agree, but tag it latest so it is easy to find
Disagree: promote the exact digest that was tested; a rebuild can produce different bytes (moved base tag, new transitive deps)
It does not matter: the same commit always produces the same image
qs.e: Builds are rarely reproducible: FROM node:22-slim may now point at a newer image, and package registries change. Only the digest guarantees that production runs what staging tested. Patching is a new build that goes through staging again.

qs.s: This Deployment runs in production. A bad build was pushed as latest and the pods restarted onto it. You run kubectl rollout undo deploy/api. What happens?

code.title: deployment.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api:latest

o: Kubernetes restores the previous image from its own cache
The undo fails because latest deployments cannot be undone
The previous pod template also says :latest, so the “rolled back” pods pull the current (bad) image again; nothing is fixed
The registry automatically serves the previous latest to rollback requests
qs.e: Rollout undo restores the previous pod template, which is a reference, not image bytes. With a moving tag the reference is the same before and after. With :latest the default pull policy is Always, so every new pod pulls the bad image. Deploy by SHA tag or digest so rollback means something.

qs.s: Pods in the new namespace prod-eu fail to start. The same Deployment works in staging. Read the events. Most likely cause?

code.title: kubectl describe pod -n prod-eu (events)
code.src:
Warning  Failed   kubelet  Failed to pull image "ghcr.io/acme/api:3f9a2c1": failed to resolve reference
  "ghcr.io/acme/api:3f9a2c1": failed to authorize: failed to fetch anonymous token:
  unexpected status from GET request to https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository%3Aacme%2Fapi%3Apull: 401 Unauthorized
Warning  Failed   kubelet  Error: ErrImagePull
Normal   BackOff  kubelet  Back-off pulling image "ghcr.io/acme/api:3f9a2c1"
Warning  Failed   kubelet  Error: ImagePullBackOff

o: The pull secret exists only in staging. Secrets are namespaced, so prod-eu pulls anonymously and the private package returns 401; create the secret there and reference it in imagePullSecrets or the ServiceAccount
The tag 3f9a2c1 does not exist in the registry
GHCR rate-limited the cluster
The nodes in prod-eu have no internet access
qs.e: “failed to fetch anonymous token … 401” means no credentials were sent for a private repository. A missing tag gives not found, and no network gives a timeout or DNS error, not an HTTP 401. Pull secrets are namespaced; many teams attach them to the namespace's default ServiceAccount, or use node-level credentials (for example ECR with node IAM).

qs.s: Your ECR lifecycle rule is “keep the last 20 images”. CI pushes an image for every pull request, about 15 per day, into the same repository. You release on Monday. The next Monday's release is broken. Can you roll back to last Monday's image?
o: Yes: lifecycle rules never delete images that ran in production
Yes: ECR keeps deleted images for 30 days
Only if you rebuild it from the old commit
No: at 15 pushes per day, the last 20 images cover only about 1.3 days, so last Monday's image was deleted days ago
qs.e: 20 / 15 ≈ 1.3 days of history. Lifecycle rules do not know what is deployed. Keep release images in a separate repository or match them with a tag-prefix rule (for example keep release-* for 90 days). Rebuilding is tempting, but it gives different bytes from the image you tested.

qs.s: Your ECR repository has tag immutability turned on. A CI job is re-run for the same commit and its push fails with the message below. What is the right response?

code.title: CI log
code.src:
$ docker push 1234567890.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/api:3f9a2c1d8e7b
The push refers to repository [1234567890.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/api]
tag invalid: The image tag '3f9a2c1d8e7b' already exists in the 'api' repository
and cannot be overwritten because the repository is immutable.

o: Turn tag immutability off so re-runs can overwrite
Make the job idempotent: if the tag already exists, skip the push and deploy the existing digest. The error is protecting the image you already tested
Delete the old tag, then push again
Push the image as latest instead
qs.e: The same commit already has an image, possibly already tested and deployed. Overwriting it (by turning immutability off or deleting the tag) would change what that tag means. Check with aws ecr describe-images or docker buildx imagetools inspect and skip the push. Pushing latest brings back the traceability problem.

interview.q: How do you guarantee that the image running in production is exactly the one you tested?
answer: Build once in CI, tag with the git SHA, and record the digest that the push returns.
Promote by digest: staging and production manifests reference image@sha256:… (or a SHA tag in a repository with immutable tags). Never rebuild for production.
Make the registry enforce it: tag immutability, and retention rules that keep release images.
Sign the image (cosign, keyless with the CI's OIDC identity) and verify signatures at admission (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller), so only CI-built images run.
Audit: kubectl get pods -o jsonpath on imageID shows the exact digest each pod runs.
followups: What does signing protect against that digests do not?
How do you patch a base image CVE under this model?

interview.q: Design the registry setup for 40 services running on EKS in two regions.
answer: ECR per account, one repository per service, with immutable tags and cross-region replication so each region pulls locally (faster, and survives a regional registry problem).
Pull-through cache rules for Docker Hub, GHCR and Quay base images, so nodes never pull anonymously from public registries.
Lifecycle rules: delete untagged images after a few days, expire PR builds, keep release tags much longer.
Scanning on push plus a CI gate on new critical CVEs; signing in CI and verification at admission for production namespaces.
IAM: nodes or workloads get pull-only access; only the CI role can push; no long-lived registry passwords.
followups: How would you handle multi-arch for Graviton nodes?
What happens to deploys if ECR in one region is down?

interview.q: During a traffic spike, new nodes could not pull images because of Docker Hub rate limits. What actions go in the postmortem?
answer: Root cause: anonymous pulls from one NAT IP; Docker Hub allows 100 pulls per 6 hours per IP for unauthenticated users, and scale-up multiplies pulls.
Immediate: authenticate pulls, or switch image references to a mirror or pull-through cache in your own registry.
Structural: no production workload references Docker Hub directly; an admission policy can enforce allowed registries.
Reduce pulls: smaller images, pre-pulled base layers on node images, and IfNotPresent with immutable tags.
Detection: alert on ImagePullBackOff counts and pull errors, because this failure shows up exactly when capacity is needed.
followups: Why does this tend to fail during scale-up and not during normal deploys?
Would you pre-bake images into node AMIs?
