one: A system that runs containers across a fleet of machines and keeps reality matching what you declared: "I want 5 copies of this, reachable at this name".
an: Not a collection of Dockers. It is an air-traffic controller for containers. You file a flight plan (YAML), and it keeps assigning planes to runways, replacing any that crash, without you touching individual planes.
how: You do not tell Kubernetes what to do; you tell it what should exist (declarative). Controllers run a loop forever: compare desired state to actual state, act to close the gap. Kill a pod and a controller notices one is missing and creates another.
Cluster = control plane + worker nodes (VMs). Each node runs a kubelet agent and a container runtime (containerd, not Docker itself, these days).

Core objects: Pod (smallest unit, one or more containers), Deployment (keeps N pod replicas, does rolling updates), Service (stable name and IP in front of changing pods), Ingress (HTTP routing from outside), ConfigMap/Secret (config), Namespace (grouping), HPA (autoscaling).
Managed offerings (EKS, GKE, AKS) run the control plane for you.
why: When you have many services, many replicas and many machines, someone has to schedule them, restart them, roll them out gradually, scale them and route traffic. Kubernetes is the standard tool for that, and its concepts show up in every senior infra conversation.
trade: It is complex. A team with three services and modest traffic is often better off on a PaaS (Render, Fly, Cloud Run, ECS, Railway). Kubernetes pays off with many services, a platform team, or portability needs.

myth.m: Kubernetes is a collection of Docker containers.
myth.r: It is an orchestrator: an API plus control loops that schedule, heal, scale and connect containers across machines. The containers are the cargo; Kubernetes is the logistics company.

q.s: You delete a pod managed by a Deployment with replicas: 3. A few seconds later there are 3 pods again. What did that?
o: Docker restarted it
The Deployment's controller saw actual (2) ≠ desired (3) and created a new pod
The load balancer
etcd copied it
q.e: Reconciliation loops are the core idea. To really remove pods you change the desired state (scale the Deployment), not the pods.

more: Labels and selectors: how everything finds everything
StatefulSets for databases and stable identities
lab: Install kind and kubectl; create a cluster with kind create cluster.
Run kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3, then kubectl get pods -o wide.
Delete a pod and watch it come back: kubectl get pods -w.
Expose it: kubectl expose deployment web --port=80, then kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 and open localhost:8080.
Change the image tag and watch the rolling update with kubectl rollout status; undo it with kubectl rollout undo.

plain:
Kubernetes runs your containers across a group of machines and keeps them running the way you described.

You do not give it commands like “start a container on server 3”. You write a description of what you want: “run 3 copies of my API, version 1.4, reachable at the name api”. Kubernetes then works constantly to make reality match that description. If a container crashes or a machine dies, it notices the difference and fixes it.

So it is not a collection of Dockers. It is the manager that decides where containers run, restarts them, scales them, updates them gradually and connects them to each other.
bridge: React is declarative: you describe what the UI should look like for the current state, and React figures out the DOM changes. Kubernetes is the same idea for servers: you describe the desired state in YAML, and Kubernetes figures out which containers to start, stop or move.

walk.title: What happens when you deploy version 1.5 of your API
steps: You change image: api:1.4 to image: api:1.5 in your Deployment file and run kubectl apply.
The API server stores the new desired state: 3 copies of 1.5.
The Deployment controller sees “desired: 3 × v1.5, actual: 3 × v1.4” and starts one new v1.5 pod.
The scheduler picks a machine (node) with free CPU and memory for it. The kubelet on that machine starts the container.
When the new pod passes its readiness check, the Service starts sending it traffic, and one old pod is stopped. This repeats until all 3 are v1.5.
If the new pods crash, the rollout stops and the old pods keep serving. kubectl rollout undo goes back.

terms: The group of machines Kubernetes manages.
One machine (usually a VM) in the cluster.
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers together.
Keeps N copies of a pod running and handles updates.
A stable name and address in front of a changing set of pods.
The “brain”: API server, scheduler, controllers, and the database (etcd).
insights: The core idea is the reconciliation loop: compare desired and actual state, act, repeat forever. Everything else builds on it.
To change anything, change the desired state (YAML), not individual pods. Deleted pods simply come back.

Most of Kubernetes is one pattern repeated: an object stored in the API server and a controller that watches it. HPA, Jobs and custom resources (CRDs) all work this way, so new objects are easy to learn once you see it.

prod.summary: In production, Kubernetes is usually a managed control plane (EKS, GKE, AKS) plus node pools you pay for. The day-to-day senior concerns are capacity (requests vs real usage), upgrades (three minor releases a year, each supported for about 14 months, with API removals), access control (RBAC, who can kubectl into prod), and knowing how to triage a broken workload from events, describe and logs.
checklist: Every workload sets CPU and memory requests based on measured usage; namespaces have ResourceQuotas so one team cannot eat the cluster.
Deploys go through CI or GitOps; humans do not kubectl apply or kubectl edit in production.
There is an upgrade plan: the cluster is within the provider's standard support window, and manifests are checked for removed APIs before each minor upgrade.
Critical services run at least 2 replicas spread across zones (topologySpreadConstraints) with a PodDisruptionBudget, so node drains and zone failures do not take them down.
RBAC follows least privilege; app ServiceAccounts cannot read Secrets of other apps; cloud access uses workload identity, not static keys in Secrets.
Cluster-level metrics and alerts exist for pending pods, node NotReady, and pods in CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled.
numbers: Kubernetes' tested limits: up to 5,000 nodes, 150,000 pods per cluster, and no more than 110 pods per node (kubernetes.io, Considerations for large clusters).
Kubernetes ships about three minor versions per year; each gets roughly 14 months of patch support (12 months plus a 2-month upgrade period).
Amazon EKS charges $0.10 per cluster-hour in standard support and $0.60 per cluster-hour in extended support, so an un-upgraded cluster costs six times more.
By default, pods tolerate a NotReady or unreachable node for 300 seconds before they are evicted and replaced elsewhere.
failures: Pods stuck in Pending with event 0/6 nodes are available: 6 Insufficient memory, although dashboards show nodes at 40% memory use.
The scheduler uses requests, not real usage. Requests are inflated. Right-size requests from metrics, or add nodes / enable the cluster autoscaler.
After a minor upgrade, CI fails with no matches for kind "CronJob" in version "batch/v1beta1".
That API version was removed (CronJob batch/v1beta1 in 1.25). Read the deprecated API migration guide before every upgrade and scan manifests with a tool such as pluto or kubent.
Pod status CrashLoopBackOff, restarts climbing, and kubectl logs is empty.

Logs show the current, just-started container. Use kubectl logs --previous and kubectl describe pod (look at Last State, exit code and Events). Exit 137 with reason OOMKilled means memory limit; exit 1 means the app crashed, often missing config.
A node fails and its pods take about 5 minutes to come back elsewhere.
Default 300 s tolerations for unreachable nodes, plus detection time. Run enough replicas across nodes and zones so losing one node does not matter while replacements start.

code.title: Triage a broken workload in five commands
code.src:
# 1. What is wrong, cluster-wide, most recent last
kubectl get events -n shop --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20

# 2. Pod state, restarts, which node
kubectl get pods -n shop -l app=orders-api -o wide

# 3. Why: Last State, exit code, OOMKilled, probe failures, scheduling
kubectl describe pod -n shop orders-api-7d9c5b7f6d-x2k8p

# 4. Logs of the crashed container, not the fresh one
kubectl logs -n shop orders-api-7d9c5b7f6d-x2k8p --previous

# 5. Is a rollout stuck? Undo it.
kubectl rollout status deploy/orders-api -n shop --timeout=60s
kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders-api -n shop

# Bonus: real usage vs requests (needs metrics-server)
kubectl top pods -n shop
code.note: describe plus logs --previous answers most incidents. Events are kept only for a short time (one hour by default), so look early.

qs.s: New pods stay Pending with 0/6 nodes are available: 6 Insufficient memory. Monitoring shows every node at about 40% memory used. What explains this?
o: A memory leak on the nodes that monitoring cannot see
etcd has run out of space
The scheduler places pods by requests; the sum of requests is full even though real usage is low
Memory limits are set too low
qs.e: Scheduling is a booking system: requests reserve capacity whether or not it is used. Over-requested pods waste nodes. Right-size requests from real usage. Limits do not affect scheduling.

qs.s: After upgrading the cluster one minor version, kubectl apply fails: no matches for kind "CronJob" in version "batch/v1beta1". What happened?
o: That API version was removed in the new Kubernetes version; the manifest must use batch/v1
The CronJob CRD was not installed
Your kubectl is older than the cluster
The namespace was deleted during the upgrade
qs.e: Kubernetes deprecates beta APIs and later removes them. Upgrades are where this bites. Check the deprecated API migration guide and scan manifests and Helm charts before upgrading.

qs.s: A node dies. It was running 2 pods from a Deployment and 1 pod created with kubectl run (no controller). What happens next?
o: All 3 pods are recreated on other nodes within seconds
Nothing is recreated until the node comes back
Only the kubectl run pod is recreated, because it has no owner
The Deployment's pods are recreated on other nodes after the node is marked unreachable (about 5 minutes by default); the bare pod is gone for good
qs.e: Only controllers recreate pods; a bare pod has nobody watching it. And it is not instant: pods tolerate an unreachable node for 300 s by default before eviction. That is why you run several replicas.

qs.s: A Deployment in namespace team-a shows 0/3 ready and no pods exist at all. Read the output. What is wrong?

code.title: kubectl output
code.src:
$ kubectl get deploy web -n team-a
NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
web    0/3     0            0           4m

$ kubectl get pods -n team-a -l app=web
No resources found in team-a namespace.

$ kubectl describe rs -n team-a web-6b7f9c   # events
Warning  FailedCreate  replicaset-controller  Error creating: pods "web-6b7f9c-x8k2p" is forbidden:
  failed quota: team-a-quota: must specify requests.cpu for: web; requests.memory for: web

o: The image cannot be pulled
The namespace has a ResourceQuota on CPU and memory requests, and the pod template has no requests, so the API server rejects every pod; add requests or a LimitRange with defaults
No node has enough free memory, so the scheduler cannot place the pods
Your user lacks RBAC permission to create pods
qs.e: No pods exist, so it is not an image or scheduling problem: those happen to pods that already exist (ImagePullBackOff, Pending). The ReplicaSet controller creates the pods, not your user, so your RBAC is not involved. Quota errors appear only on the ReplicaSet events, which is why people miss them.

qs.s: You need to drain a node for an upgrade. kubectl drain keeps printing the message below and never finishes. The Deployment has replicas: 2. Why?

code.title: pdb.yaml + drain output
code.src:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
# $ kubectl drain node-7 --ignore-daemonsets
# error when evicting pods/"api-5d8f-k2x9q" -n shop (will retry after 5s):
#   Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.

o: Drain cannot evict pods that belong to a Deployment
The PDB needs maxUnavailable as well as minAvailable
--ignore-daemonsets also blocks Deployment pods
With 2 replicas and minAvailable: 2, zero voluntary disruptions are allowed, so eviction is refused forever; run 3 replicas or use maxUnavailable: 1
qs.e: A PDB limits voluntary evictions such as drains. minAvailable equal to the replica count means “never evict”. Check kubectl get pdb: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS is 0. A PDB uses one of the two fields, not both. This mistake blocks cluster upgrades and node autoscaler scale-down.

qs.s: Your managed Kubernetes control plane (API server) is unavailable for 20 minutes. What happens to the apps already running?
o: All pods stop, because kubelets need the API server to keep containers running
Services stop routing, because kube-proxy loses its rules
Running pods keep running and serving through existing Service rules, but nothing changes: no deploys, no scaling, no rescheduling of failed pods
Pods keep running, but all of their DNS lookups fail at once
qs.e: The data plane works without the control plane for a while. Kubelets keep running their pods, kube-proxy keeps the last rules, and CoreDNS keeps serving from its cache of known Services. What stops is reconciliation: crashed pods on a failed node are not replaced, the HPA cannot scale, and deploys fail. This is why control plane availability matters most during incidents.

qs.s: An API runs in 3 zones with pods spread evenly. Each pod handles 100 requests per second at most. Peak traffic is 450 rps. What is the smallest replica count (a multiple of 3) that still handles peak if one zone fails, without waiting for new pods?
qs.e: Losing one zone leaves 2/3 of pods. With 6 replicas, 4 remain = 400 rps, below 450. With 9, 6 remain = 600 rps, which is enough. 12 also works but is not the smallest. 8 cannot be split evenly. The real lesson: N+1 at the zone level costs 50% more capacity with 3 zones.

interview.q: Explain what happens from kubectl apply of a Deployment until a new pod is serving traffic.
answer: kubectl sends the object to the API server; it authenticates, authorizes (RBAC), runs admission (defaults, policies, quotas) and stores it in etcd.
The Deployment controller sees a new pod template and creates or scales a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates Pod objects.
The scheduler picks a node using requests, affinity, taints and topology spread, and writes the node name on the pod.
The kubelet on that node pulls the image, sets up the network via the CNI plugin, starts containers and runs probes.

When readiness passes, the pod is added to the Service's EndpointSlices; kube-proxy (or the CNI's eBPF data plane) and ingress controllers start routing to it. The rolling update then removes an old pod.

interview.q: When would you tell a team not to use Kubernetes?
answer: A few services, a small team and no platform engineers: a PaaS (Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Render, Fly) gives deploys, scaling and TLS with far less to operate.
Kubernetes costs real time: three minor releases a year with API removals, add-ons to maintain (ingress or gateway, cert-manager, autoscaler, observability), and RBAC and network policy to own.
It pays off with many services, several teams sharing a platform, special scheduling needs (GPUs, batch), or a need for portability across clouds.
A middle path: managed Kubernetes with a small set of opinionated templates, or GKE Autopilot / EKS Auto Mode to remove node management.
Decide on numbers: engineer hours per month for operations versus what the team would spend on PaaS limitations.
followups: What signs tell you a team has outgrown its PaaS?
What would you put in a minimal production cluster?

interview.q: How do you upgrade a production cluster by one minor version safely?
answer: Read the release notes and the deprecated API migration guide; scan manifests, Helm charts and live objects for removed APIs (pluto, kubent).
Upgrade a staging cluster first and run the real deploy pipeline and smoke tests against it.
Upgrade the control plane, then node pools one at a time: surge new nodes, cordon and drain old ones. PDBs and multiple replicas keep apps available during drains.
Check add-ons (CNI, CSI, ingress or gateway, autoscaler) for compatibility with the new version before, not after.

Watch pending pods, error rates and node readiness during the roll; keep each step small so you can stop. Staying within standard support avoids extended-support fees (on EKS, $0.60 instead of $0.10 per cluster-hour).
followups: What do you do if a PDB blocks the drain?
How far can the kubelet lag behind the API server?

flowchart TD U["kubectl apply
deployment.yaml"] --> API["API server"] API <--> ETCD[("etcd
stored desired state")] CTRL["Deployment controller"] -->|watch| API CTRL --> CMP{"desired = actual?"} CMP -->|"no: want 3, have 2"| FIX["create 1 pod"] FIX --> API CMP -->|yes| WAIT["wait for next change"] WAIT --> CMP SCH[Scheduler] -->|"pick node for pod"| API KL["kubelet on each node"] -->|"watch: my pods"| API KL --> RUN["start containers

diagrams.title: Rolling out api:1.5 (3 replicas)
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant You
  participant API as API server
  participant DC as Deployment controller
  participant S as Scheduler
  participant K as kubelet
  You->>API: kubectl apply (image api:1.5)
  API-->>DC: desired state changed
  Note over DC: desired 3 x v1.5, actual 3 x v1.4
  loop until all 3 pods run v1.5
    DC->>API: create 1 new v1.5 pod
    API-->>S: pod has no node yet
    S->>API: bind pod to a node with free CPU and memory
    API-->>K: new pod for this node
    K->>K: start container, run readiness probe
    K->>API: pod is Ready
    Note over API: Service now sends it traffic
    DC->>API: stop 1 old v1.4 pod
  end
diagrams.caption: What to notice: this is the walk-through above as messages. If a new pod never becomes Ready, the loop stops and the old pods keep serving until you fix it or run kubectl rollout undo.

one: The four Kubernetes objects you meet first: where code runs, how many copies, how to find them, and how outside traffic gets in.
an: Pods are workers. A Deployment is the manager who keeps headcount at N. A Service is the department's phone extension that rings whichever worker is free. Ingress is the building's front desk routing visitors to departments.
how: Pod: one or more containers sharing a network IP and volumes. Pods are disposable; they get new IPs every time they are recreated. Never address a pod directly.

Deployment → manages a ReplicaSet → manages pods. Changing the pod template (for example the image) triggers a rolling update: new pods start, pass readiness checks, old ones stop. Defaults: maxSurge 25%, maxUnavailable 25%.

Service: a stable virtual IP and DNS name (api.default.svc.cluster.local) that load-balances to ready pods matching a label selector. The current pod list lives in EndpointSlices. Types: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud LB), ExternalName.

Ingress: host/path rules (api.acme.com/v1 → api Service) and TLS, run by an ingress controller. The Ingress API is frozen and the Kubernetes project now recommends the Gateway API. The popular ingress-nginx controller was retired in March 2026 and gets no more security fixes, so new setups should use Gateway API or another maintained controller.

Probes: startup (wait for slow boot before other probes run), readiness (do not send me traffic yet), liveness (restart me if this fails). Resource requests (for scheduling) and limits (hard cap: over the memory limit = OOMKilled; over the CPU limit = throttled, not killed).
why: Almost every Kubernetes incident is one of these misconfigured: wrong selector, missing readiness probe, memory limit too low.
trade: A liveness probe that checks the database will restart every pod when the DB blips, turning a small outage into a big one. Liveness should check only the process itself.

myth.m: Readiness and liveness probes are the same check.
myth.r: Readiness gates traffic; liveness triggers restarts. Mixing them up causes restart storms.

q.s: Pods show status OOMKilled and restart every few minutes under load. What is happening?
o: The liveness probe is wrong
The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it
Ingress misrouting
Service selector mismatch
q.e: Raise the limit to fit real usage, or find the memory leak. Check usage with metrics first.

plain:
Four Kubernetes objects cover most daily work. A Pod is where your container runs. A Deployment keeps the right number of pods running and replaces them during updates. A Service gives those pods one stable name and spreads traffic among them. An Ingress (or Gateway) routes outside web traffic to Services.

Pods come and go and change addresses constantly. That is why everything talks to Services, never directly to pods.
bridge: Compare with React: a pod is like a component instance (created and destroyed often), the Deployment is like the parent that decides how many to render, and the Service is a stable prop name other parts use, no matter which instances exist right now.

walk.title: A request from the internet to your pod
steps: A user requests https://api.shop.com/orders.
The cloud load balancer sends it to the ingress or gateway controller running inside the cluster (for example Envoy Gateway, Traefik or a cloud provider's controller).
A routing rule (an Ingress, or an HTTPRoute in Gateway API) says api.shop.com → Service orders-api, port 80.
The Service knows which pods currently match its label app=orders-api and are passing readiness checks (listed in its EndpointSlices), and traffic goes to one of them.
The pod's container answers on the Service's targetPort. If that pod had failed its readiness probe, it would not be in the list and would get no traffic.

terms: Tags on pods, and the rule a Service or Deployment uses to find them.
“Can I receive traffic now?” Failing removes the pod from the Service.
“Am I stuck?” Failing restarts the container.
Reserved resources for scheduling / hard maximums (exceed memory = killed).
Rules for routing outside HTTP traffic to Services.
insights: Labels are the glue. A Deployment finds its pods, and a Service finds its endpoints, only by matching labels. One typo and traffic goes nowhere.
A rollout is only as safe as the readiness probe. If readiness passes before the app can really serve, Kubernetes sends traffic to a pod that fails.
Memory over the limit kills the container; CPU over the limit only slows it down. That is why many teams set memory limits but skip CPU limits.

prod.summary: Most Kubernetes incidents are small mistakes in these objects: a selector that matches nothing, a liveness probe that restarts healthy pods, a memory limit below real usage, or a rollout that drops requests because pods exit before traffic stops. A senior reads a Deployment YAML and checks probes, resources, shutdown and labels before anything else.
checklist: Service selector exactly matches the pod template labels; kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api shows ready endpoints.
Readiness probe checks “can I serve now” (including critical dependencies if you choose); liveness checks only the process itself; slow starters have a startup probe.
Memory request = limit for predictable behaviour; memory limit is above the measured peak with headroom. CPU limits are used carefully because they cause throttling.
Graceful shutdown: app handles SIGTERM, a short preStop sleep lets endpoints update, and terminationGracePeriodSeconds is longer than the longest request.
At least 2 replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget for anything user-facing.
Image is pinned by SHA tag or digest, and config comes from ConfigMaps/Secrets, not baked in.
numbers: Probe defaults: periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3. A 1-second timeout is easy to miss under load.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds defaults to 30; after that the kubelet sends SIGKILL.
Rolling update rounding: maxSurge percentages round up and maxUnavailable percentages round down. With 10 replicas and 25%/25%: at most 13 pods, at least 8 available.
CrashLoopBackOff restart delay doubles from 10 s and is capped at 5 minutes.
failures: Ingress returns 503 for a new service; kubectl get endpointslices for it lists no addresses.
The Service selector does not match the pod labels (for example app: orders-api vs app: orders), or no pod is ready. Compare kubectl get pods --show-labels with the selector.
Pods show OOMKilled, exit code 137, and restart every few minutes under load.
Usage exceeded the memory limit. Check kubectl top pod and history, raise the limit to the real peak plus headroom, or fix the leak. For Node, also set --max-old-space-size below the limit.
About 1% of requests get 502 for a few seconds during every rollout.
Pods exit on SIGTERM while the ingress or kube-proxy still routes to them. Add preStop: sleep 5 (native sleep action or exec), then drain in-flight requests before exit.
A slow-starting Java/Next.js pod is restarted forever and never becomes ready.
The liveness probe fails during boot and kills the container. Add a startupProbe with enough failureThreshold × periodSeconds to cover start time.
During a database blip, every API pod restarts at once and the outage gets longer.
Liveness probe checks the database. Liveness must check only the process; let readiness (or the app) handle dependencies.

code.title: Deployment + Service with probes, resources and graceful shutdown
code.src:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-api }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:3f9a2c1d8e7b
          ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 384Mi }
            limits: { memory: 384Mi }
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 3000 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 24
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 3000 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 3000 }
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep: { seconds: 5 }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  selector: { app: orders-api }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 3000 }]
code.note: The selector and labels must match exactly. The startup probe allows up to 120 s of boot. No CPU limit avoids throttling; the memory limit equals the request. The native preStop sleep action is available in current Kubernetes; on older clusters use exec: ["sleep", "5"].

qs.s: Service orders has selector: { app: orders-api }. The Deployment's pod template has labels: { app: orders, tier: api }. Pods are Running and Ready. What do users see?
o: Everything works, because the Deployment name matches
Traffic goes to random pods in the namespace
Requests work but are slow, because of label lookups
The Service has no endpoints, so the ingress returns 503
qs.e: A Service finds pods only by label selector. app: orders-api matches no pod, so its EndpointSlices are empty. The Deployment name plays no role in routing.

qs.s: Readiness probes are correct, yet about 1% of requests fail with 502 for a few seconds during every rolling update. Most likely cause?
o: maxSurge is set too high
Terminating pods exit right away on SIGTERM while the ingress and kube-proxy are still sending them traffic; add a short preStop sleep and drain requests
The liveness probe is too strict
Image pulls are slow on the new nodes
qs.e: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, and load balancers update a moment later. A pod that exits instantly drops those last requests. Slow pulls delay the rollout but do not cause 502s, because old pods keep serving.

qs.s: A Deployment has replicas: 10 and the default rolling update strategy (25% surge, 25% unavailable). During a rollout, what is the maximum total pods and the minimum available pods?
o: 12 total, 8 available
13 total, 7 available
13 total, 8 available
10 total, 10 available
qs.e: 25% of 10 is 2.5. maxSurge rounds up to 3, so up to 13 pods. maxUnavailable rounds down to 2, so at least 8 available. Capacity planning must allow for the 3 extra pods.

qs.s: A Node API has limits: { cpu: 500m }. Average CPU is about 30% of the limit, but p99 latency is 400 ms instead of 60 ms. You read cpu.stat inside the container. What is the most likely cause?

code.title: /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat
code.src:
usage_usec 81234567
user_usec 70112003
system_usec 11122564
nr_periods 50211
nr_throttled 21877
throttled_usec 1843000000

o: The HPA is not scaling out fast enough
The memory limit is too close to usage, so GC runs constantly
The liveness probe restarts the pod during traffic peaks
CPU throttling: in about 44% of 100 ms periods the pod used its 50 ms quota early and had to wait; raise or remove the CPU limit and keep the request
qs.e: 21877 / 50211 ≈ 44% of periods were throttled, and the total wait was about 1,843 s. Short bursts hit the quota even when the average is low. The HPA is tempting, but it scales on average usage (30% here), so it would not react. Restarts would show in the restart count, and GC pressure would show in memory metrics.

qs.s: Pods are Running and Ready. kubectl get endpointslices for the Service lists 3 addresses. Yet curl http://orders-api from another pod gives connection refused. Find the bug.

code.title: service.yaml + container port
code.src:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  selector: { app: orders-api }
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
# in the Deployment's container spec:
# ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
# readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 3000 } }

o: The selector does not match the pods
targetPort is 8080 but the app listens on 3000; traffic reaches the pods on a port where nothing listens
port: 80 needs root, so the Service cannot open it
The readiness probe should use port 80
qs.e: Endpoints exist, so the selector matches and readiness passes (the probe checks 3000 directly). The Service then forwards to podIP:8080, which refuses the connection. A Service port is a virtual port handled by kube-proxy, so port 80 needs no root. Use named ports (targetPort: http) to avoid this mismatch.

qs.s: Requests to /api/orders get 404 from the ingress, while /api works. Which change fixes it?

code.title: ingress.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
spec:
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Exact
            backend:
              service:
                name: orders-api
                port: { number: 80 }

o: Change pathType to Prefix, which matches /api and everything under /api/
Change the path to /api/*
Add a trailing slash: /api/
Move the rule to a different namespace
qs.e: Exact matches only the exact path. Prefix matches by path elements, so /api also matches /api/orders but not /apiv2. A * wildcard is not part of the Ingress spec; how it behaves depends on the controller. Gateway API's PathPrefix works the same way as Prefix.

qs.s: A pod has terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 and a preStop sleep of 5 s. A 40-second report export starts just before the pod is told to terminate. The app drains requests correctly on SIGTERM. What happens to the export?
o: It finishes: the grace period starts after the preStop hook ends
It finishes: Kubernetes waits for open connections before sending SIGKILL
It is cut off: the 30 s count starts before preStop, so the app gets SIGTERM at 5 s and SIGKILL at 30 s; set the grace period above 5 + 40 s, or move long work to a job queue
It is cut off at 5 s, when preStop ends
qs.e: The Kubernetes docs say the grace period countdown begins before the preStop hook runs. So the timeline is: preStop 0–5 s, SIGTERM at 5 s, SIGKILL at 30 s. The export needs until 40 s. Kubernetes never waits for connections on its own. Long jobs are usually better as queued work than as HTTP requests.

interview.q: Design the readiness, liveness and startup probes for a Node API that depends on Postgres.
answer: Liveness checks only the process: is the event loop responsive (a trivial /healthz)? Never the database, or a DB blip restarts every pod at once.

Readiness answers “should I get traffic now?”: false during startup, during shutdown (after SIGTERM), and optionally when a critical dependency is down. If every pod depends on the same DB, failing readiness on all of them only turns errors into 503s, so many teams keep the DB out of readiness too and handle it in the app.
Startup probe for slow boots (migrations check, cache warm-up), with failureThreshold × periodSeconds covering the worst start time; liveness and readiness wait for it.
Timeouts: the default timeoutSeconds is 1 s; a busy event loop can miss it. Keep probe handlers cheap and set timeouts deliberately.
Test it: kill the DB in staging and watch whether pods restart (bad) or report errors and recover (good).
followups: Should readiness fail when Redis (a cache) is down?
How would you detect a deadlocked worker that still answers HTTP?

interview.q: How do you choose CPU and memory requests and limits for a service?
answer: Start from measurements: p95–p99 memory and typical CPU from metrics under real load, not guesses.
Memory: request = limit, set above the measured peak with headroom; going over the limit means OOMKilled, so runtime heap settings must fit inside it.
CPU: the request decides scheduling and the share under contention; a CPU limit causes throttling. Latency-sensitive services often run with a request and no CPU limit.
Requests that are too high waste nodes (pods Pending while nodes are mostly idle); too low causes noisy-neighbour problems and evictions under memory pressure.
Review regularly with VPA recommendations or similar, and enforce defaults per namespace with LimitRange and ResourceQuota.
followups: What QoS class does a pod with request = limit get, and why does it matter?
How do requests interact with the HPA's target utilization?

interview.q: Walk me through a zero-downtime rolling update. What can still go wrong?
answer: The Deployment creates new pods (up to maxSurge) and removes old ones (keeping availability above replicas − maxUnavailable), moving only when new pods are Ready.
Readiness must reflect real ability to serve; otherwise traffic hits pods that are still warming up.
On the way out: endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so a short preStop sleep plus in-app draining avoids 502s; the grace period must cover preStop plus the longest request.
Compatibility: during the rollout, old and new versions run together, so DB schema and API changes must be backward compatible (expand/contract).
Safety: minReadySeconds and progressDeadlineSeconds catch bad rollouts; a PDB and enough spare capacity for the surge pods keep the rollout from stalling.
followups: How would you roll out a breaking database migration?
When would you choose a canary over a rolling update?

one: Helm packages Kubernetes YAML into templated, versioned "charts" so you can install and configure apps with values instead of copy-pasting manifests.
an: A form letter with blanks. The template stays the same; staging and production fill in different values.
how: A chart = templates + a values.yaml + Chart.yaml. helm upgrade --install api ./chart -f values-prod.yaml renders the templates with those values, applies them, and stores a numbered release revision so you can roll back.
Helm does not wait for pods by default. In Helm 4, --wait waits until resources are ready, and --rollback-on-failure (called --atomic in Helm 3) rolls back automatically if they are not.
Alternatives: Kustomize (patch overlays on plain YAML, built into kubectl). It suits in-house apps with small per-environment differences; Helm suits packaged, reusable charts.

GitOps (Argo CD, Flux): the cluster continuously syncs itself to what is in a Git repo. Deploy = merge a PR; drift from manual changes is detected and reverted. Argo CD renders Helm charts itself, so Helm becomes a templating tool there.
why: Real apps need dozens of YAML objects per environment. Without templating and GitOps, environments drift apart and nobody knows what is actually deployed.
trade: Heavily templated charts become unreadable. Keep them boring.

myth.m: kubectl apply from my laptop is how we deploy.
myth.r: It works until two people do it differently. GitOps makes the repo the single source of truth and gives you an audit log.

q.s: What does GitOps add over running helm upgrade from CI?
o: Faster builds
The cluster pulls and continuously reconciles to Git, so manual drift is detected and reverted
Smaller images
Free hosting
q.e: Pull-based continuous reconciliation is the key difference. Git becomes the desired state, mirroring how Kubernetes itself works.

more: Argo CD Applications and sync waves
Secrets in GitOps (Sealed Secrets, External Secrets, SOPS)
lab: helm create mychart, read every generated file, and install it on kind.
Make two values files (staging, prod) with different replica counts and install both into separate namespaces.
Install Argo CD on kind and point it at a Git repo with your manifests. Change replicas in Git and watch it sync.

plain:
A real app in Kubernetes needs many YAML files, and each environment (staging, production) needs slightly different values. Helm turns those files into templates with a values file, so you install the same “chart” with different settings.

GitOps tools (Argo CD, Flux) go one step further: the cluster watches a Git repository and automatically makes itself match it.
bridge: A Helm chart is like a React component for infrastructure: one template, different props (values) per environment.

walk.title: Deploying with GitOps
steps: Your Git repo holds the chart and values-prod.yaml with image.tag: 3f9a2c1 and replicas: 4.
CI builds a new image 8be41d0 and opens a PR changing the tag in values-prod.yaml.
A teammate reviews and merges it.
Argo CD, running in the cluster, notices the repo changed and applies the new version.
Someone changes replicas by hand in the cluster. Argo CD sees the difference from Git and changes it back. Git is the truth.

terms: A Helm package: templates plus default values.
Settings that fill in the templates.
One installed copy of a chart, with history for rollback.
Git is the source of truth; the cluster syncs itself to it.
When the real system differs from what the config says.
insights: Deploying = merging a PR gives you review, history and easy rollback for free.
Keep templates boring. Clever templating logic becomes impossible to debug.
In GitOps, roll back by reverting the commit in Git. A change made only in the cluster is drift, and Argo CD with self-heal will put the bad version back.

prod.summary: In production, Helm charts are rendered either by CI (helm upgrade --install) or by a GitOps tool such as Argo CD or Flux that syncs the cluster to Git. Seniors care that a release is reproducible (pinned chart and image versions), that config changes actually roll pods, that secrets never sit in plain values files, and that a failed or interrupted deploy can be rolled back.
checklist: Chart version and image tag are pinned in Git per environment; values-prod.yaml is reviewed like code.
Changes are previewed before applying: helm diff upgrade (plugin) or the Argo CD diff view in the PR.
Pod templates carry a checksum annotation of their ConfigMap/Secret, so a config change triggers a rollout.
Secrets come from External Secrets, Sealed Secrets or SOPS, never plain in values files.
When an HPA owns replicas, the chart does not set it (or GitOps ignores that field), so Git and the autoscaler do not fight.
Charts stay simple: helm lint and helm template run in CI, and templates avoid deep logic.
numbers: Helm 4 was released on November 12, 2025. New releases default to Kubernetes server-side apply; releases created by Helm 3 keep client-side apply on upgrade.
Helm stores each release revision as a Secret (sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<N>) in the release namespace. A Secret is limited to 1 MiB, so huge charts fail to install.
helm upgrade --history-max defaults to 10 revisions kept.
failures: CI fails with Error: UPGRADE FAILED: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress.

A previous run was cancelled mid-deploy and left the release in pending-upgrade. Check helm history <release>, then helm rollback to the last deployed revision. Stop CI from killing Helm mid-run, and serialise deploys per release.
A ConfigMap value changed via helm upgrade, but pods still use the old config.
Env vars from a ConfigMap are read only at container start, and the pod template did not change, so no rollout happened. Add checksum/config annotation on the pod template.
Argo CD shows the app OutOfSync every few minutes and replicas jump between 3 and 12; latency spikes.
Git sets replicas: 3 and self-heal reverts what the HPA scaled. Remove replicas from the manifest when an HPA is used, or add an ignoreDifferences rule for it.
Install fails with Secret "sh.helm.release.v1..." is invalid: data: Too long.
The release record exceeded the 1 MiB Secret limit, usually because large files were bundled in the chart. Add a .helmignore and move big data out of the chart.

code.title: Chart template: config change triggers a rollout
code.note: The checksum/config annotation changes whenever the rendered ConfigMap changes, which changes the pod template and starts a rolling update. replicas is omitted when an HPA owns scaling.

qs.s: You change a ConfigMap value in the chart and run helm upgrade. It succeeds, but the pods keep the old value. Why?
o: The pods read the ConfigMap as env vars only at start, and the pod template did not change, so no rollout happened; add a checksum annotation
helm upgrade failed silently
etcd caches ConfigMaps for 24 hours
You must helm uninstall and install again to change config
qs.e: Helm updated the ConfigMap object, but Kubernetes only replaces pods when the pod template changes. The checksum annotation ties the two together. Uninstalling would work but causes downtime.

qs.s: A CI job was cancelled in the middle of helm upgrade. Now every deploy fails: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress. What is going on?
o: Tiller, the Helm server in the cluster, is holding a lock
The namespace must be deleted and recreated
The interrupted run left the release in a pending state; check helm history and roll back to the last deployed revision
The default timeout is too short; increase --timeout
qs.e: Helm marks the release revision as pending while it works. If the process dies, the mark stays. Tiller was removed in Helm 3, so it is not the cause. Deleting the namespace would delete the app.

qs.s: Argo CD (with self-heal) manages a Deployment that has replicas: 3 in Git and an HPA. Under load the HPA scales to 12, then replicas drop back to 3 every few minutes. Fix?
o: Raise the HPA's minReplicas to 12
Remove replicas from the Git manifest (or tell Argo CD to ignore that field) so the HPA owns it
Turn off the cluster autoscaler
Use helm rollback after each scale-up
qs.e: Two controllers own the same field: Git says 3, the HPA says 12, and self-heal keeps reverting. Give the field one owner. Raising minReplicas would hide the problem and waste capacity.

qs.s: After bumping image.tag to 1.10, pods fail with ImagePullBackOff: ghcr.io/acme/api:1.1: not found. What went wrong?

code.title: values-prod.yaml + template line
code.src:
# values-prod.yaml
image:
  repository: ghcr.io/acme/api
  tag: 1.10

# templates/deployment.yaml
#   image: {{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}

o: The registry trims trailing zeros from tags
Helm caches the previous tag
Kubernetes normalises image tags to semver
YAML reads 1.10 as the number 1.1; quote it in values (tag: "1.10") and use | quote or toString in the template
qs.e: Unquoted 1.10 is a YAML float, and the float 1.10 equals 1.1. Helm renders the number, so the tag becomes 1.1. Tags made only of digits have the same problem: 3123456 renders as 3.123456e+06. | quote in the template alone does not help (it gives "1.1"), because the value is already a number when the template runs. Always quote string values in values files.

qs.s: Read the release history. A cancelled CI job left the release stuck. Which command gets you unblocked onto the last known-good state?

code.title: helm history api -n shop
code.src:
REVISION  UPDATED                    STATUS           CHART      APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
41        Mon Sep 28 10:02:11 2026   superseded       api-2.3.0  8be41d0      Upgrade complete
42        Tue Sep 29 16:40:55 2026   deployed         api-2.3.1  c41a9e2      Upgrade complete
43        Wed Sep 30 09:12:03 2026   pending-upgrade  api-2.3.1  d7f03b5      Preparing upgrade

o: helm rollback api 41 -n shop
helm rollback api 42 -n shop
helm uninstall api -n shop, then install again
helm upgrade api ./chart --force-replace
qs.e: Revision 42 is the last one with status deployed, so it is the known-good state. Rolling back to 41 would also undo the good 42 change. Uninstalling deletes the app and causes downtime. Another upgrade fails with “another operation is in progress” while 43 is pending.

qs.s: CI runs helm upgrade --install api ./chart (Helm 4, no extra flags). The job is green, but the new pods are in CrashLoopBackOff. Why did CI not notice?
o: Helm only checks pods in the default namespace
Without --wait, Helm returns once the objects are applied; it does not wait for pods to become ready. Add --wait --rollback-on-failure and a --timeout
CrashLoopBackOff is not an error state for Helm, only for kubectl
Helm 4 waits, but only for Jobs
qs.e: Helm 4's default wait strategy is hookOnly: it waits for hooks, not for your Deployment. So “success” means “the API server accepted the objects”. With --wait Helm watches readiness until --timeout (default 5 minutes), and --rollback-on-failure (Helm 3: --atomic) restores the previous revision if it fails.

qs.s: During an incident, an engineer runs kubectl scale deploy/checkout --replicas=10. Two minutes later it is back to 4. The app is managed by this Argo CD Application. What is the right way to scale during the incident?

code.title: argocd-application.yaml
code.src:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/deploy
    path: apps/checkout
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: shop
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

o: Run kubectl scale every two minutes until the incident is over
Delete the Argo CD Application so it stops interfering
Change replicas in Git (a fast-tracked PR), or temporarily turn off self-heal for this app and record that in the incident log
Edit the ReplicaSet directly, because Argo CD only watches Deployments
qs.e: With selfHeal: true, Argo CD reverts any live change that differs from Git. Git is the way to change desired state; pausing auto-sync is the documented escape hatch, and it must be undone afterwards. Deleting the Application can delete its resources if a cascading finalizer is set. Editing the ReplicaSet fails because the Deployment controller resets it.

interview.q: Helm, Kustomize or plain manifests: how do you choose for a new platform?
answer: Third-party software (ingress or gateway controllers, cert-manager, databases operators): use the vendor's Helm chart; you configure it through values and get upgrades.
In-house services with small per-environment differences: Kustomize overlays or one simple shared chart. Avoid per-service charts full of logic.
Whatever renders the YAML, a GitOps tool (Argo CD, Flux) should apply it, so Git is the record of what runs.
Keep templates boring: few conditionals, values validated with values.schema.json, helm lint and helm template plus a schema check (kubeconform) in CI.
Review the rendered output, not only the template diff: helm diff or the Argo CD diff in the PR.
followups: How do you share one chart across 30 services without it becoming a mess?
What does Helm 4's server-side apply change for you?

interview.q: How do you handle secrets in a GitOps workflow?
answer: Plain Kubernetes Secrets in Git are only base64, not encrypted; they must never be committed.

External Secrets Operator: Git holds a reference; the operator reads the value from AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or GCP Secret Manager and creates the Secret in the cluster. Rotation happens in the secret store.
Sealed Secrets or SOPS: the encrypted value lives in Git and only the cluster (or a KMS key) can decrypt it. Simple, but rotation and key management are on you.
Combine with RBAC so only the app's ServiceAccount can read its Secrets, and with encryption at rest for etcd.
Pods must notice rotated values: mounted files update, env vars do not, so use a restart-on-change annotation or a reloader.
followups: What happens to running pods when a secret rotates?
Who should be allowed to read secrets in production?

interview.q: A helm upgrade half-failed in production. Walk me through recovery and prevention.
answer: Look first: helm history for the release status, helm status, then kubectl get pods, events and logs for what actually broke.
If the release is stuck in pending-upgrade, roll back to the last deployed revision; if pods are failing, roll back to the last good revision and confirm readiness.
Check what Helm does not roll back: database migrations run by hooks, CRDs (Helm does not upgrade or delete CRDs in crds/), and external side effects.

Prevention: --wait --rollback-on-failure with a sensible timeout, one deploy at a time per release (CI concurrency group), no cancelling a running Helm job, and a staging run of the same chart and values.
Keep enough history (--history-max defaults to 10) so the good revision is still there.
followups: How would you make a migration hook safe to re-run?
Why might a rollback itself fail?

one: An infrastructure layer (Istio, Linkerd) that handles service-to-service traffic: mTLS encryption, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and telemetry, without changing app code.
an: Every service gets a personal assistant (a sidecar proxy) who handles all its phone calls: encrypting them, redialling if dropped, and logging every call.
how: A proxy handles every call between services. Istio's classic mode uses an Envoy sidecar in each pod; Linkerd uses its own lightweight Rust proxy as a sidecar; Istio's ambient mode (stable since Istio 1.24, November 2024) removes sidecars and uses a per-node proxy (ztunnel) for mTLS, plus optional per-namespace Envoy “waypoint” proxies for HTTP features.

A control plane configures the proxies: "send 5% of traffic to v2", "retry twice with a 200ms per-try timeout", "require mTLS between everything". It also issues and rotates the certificates that give each workload an identity.

Because every call passes a proxy, you get uniform metrics (request rate, errors, latency per route) and trace spans without code changes. Apps still need to forward trace headers for traces to connect.
why: With 50 services in 5 languages, implementing retries, mTLS and metrics in each one is inconsistent. The mesh does it once.
trade: Significant operational complexity and latency/resource overhead. Most teams do not need one until they have many services and a platform team.

myth.r: Many run fine with libraries and a good load balancer. A mesh is a scaling tool for large fleets.

q.s: A team with 4 services asks whether to adopt Istio. Strongest counter-argument?
o: It cannot do mTLS
The operational cost outweighs benefits at this size; a few library-level retries/timeouts will do
It only works on Windows
It replaces the database
q.e: Adopt infrastructure for the problems you have. Revisit when the fleet and team grow.

more: Cost: latency and memory per sidecar
lab: Install Linkerd on kind (its CLI walks you through it), inject a demo app, and open the dashboard to see per-route success rates and latency without changing app code.
docs: Linkerd: What is a service mesh?

plain: When many services call each other, each one needs the same networking features: encryption, retries, timeouts, and metrics on every call. A service mesh adds a small proxy next to every service and routes all traffic through these proxies, so these features work everywhere without changing app code.
bridge: It is like adding a fetch wrapper with retries, timeouts and logging to every app in the company, except it lives outside the code, so it works for every language at once.

walk.title: Rolling out a new version to 5% of traffic
steps: The checkout service calls the pricing service. Both have a mesh proxy next to them.
You deploy pricing v2 alongside v1.
You tell the mesh: send 5% of pricing traffic to v2.
The mesh dashboard shows v2's error rate and latency next to v1's, per route, without any code changes.
v2 looks healthy; you move to 50%, then 100%. If it had failed, you would set it back to 0% in seconds.

terms: A helper container running next to your app container in the same pod.
Both sides of a connection prove their identity with certificates.
Sending percentages of traffic to different versions.
The part that configures all the proxies.
insights: Every proxy adds a little latency and memory per pod; across hundreds of pods it adds up.
A mesh is shared infrastructure: one bad policy or proxy version can break every service at once. Treat mesh changes like database migrations: staged and reversible.
Ambient mode lowers per-pod cost with one shared proxy per node, but HTTP features (retries, traffic splits) then need a waypoint proxy.

prod.summary: A mesh moves networking policy (mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splits) out of app code into proxies run by a platform team. In production it adds a new failure surface: proxy resource use per pod, start-up ordering, retry storms, and certificate or policy changes that can break all traffic at once. Seniors adopt it for a specific need (zero-trust mTLS, many languages, canaries) and roll it out namespace by namespace.
checklist: There is a concrete reason: required mTLS between services, many languages, or traffic-split canaries; not “microservices need one”.
mTLS rolls out in PERMISSIVE mode first; STRICT is enabled per namespace only after all clients are in the mesh.
Retries exist at one layer only, with a retry budget or low attempt count and per-try timeouts; app-level retries are removed where the mesh retries.
Proxy CPU and memory requests are counted in capacity planning, and sidecar mode vs ambient is chosen on purpose.
Apps start after the proxy is ready (Istio holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts, or native sidecars), and Jobs can finish.
Mesh upgrades are canaried (revisioned control planes), because a bad proxy version affects every service.
numbers: Istio 1.24 docs: at 1,000 HTTP requests per second, an Envoy sidecar with 2 worker threads uses about 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB of memory; a ztunnel uses about 0.06 vCPU and 12 MB.
Istio retries failed HTTP requests twice by default, even without any VirtualService. App-level retries on top multiply with it.
Retries multiply across hops: 3 attempts at each of 3 layers can send 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 requests to the last service for one user request.
Istio's ambient mode reached General Availability in Istio 1.24 (November 2024).
failures: After enabling STRICT mTLS, Prometheus scrapes and a legacy VM client fail with connection reset by peer.
Clients outside the mesh send plaintext, and STRICT rejects it. Use PERMISSIVE during migration, bring the clients into the mesh, or add a port-level exception for metrics.
Kubernetes Jobs with an injected sidecar never complete: the app exits 0, but the pod stays Running.

The proxy container keeps running. Use native sidecars (init containers with restartPolicy: Always, stable since Kubernetes 1.33), which Istio can inject, or tell the proxy to exit when the app finishes.
App logs ECONNREFUSED on its first DB or API call right after pod start, then works.
The app started before the sidecar proxy was ready to route traffic. Enable holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts or native sidecars.
One slow service causes a traffic spike and cascading 503s across the fleet; Envoy access logs show response flag UH or UO.

Retry amplification plus outlier detection or circuit breakers ejecting hosts (UH = no healthy upstream, UO = overflow). Cut retries to one layer, add per-try timeouts and retry budgets, and size connection pools deliberately.

code.title: Istio: 5% canary with timeout and bounded retries
code.src:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: pricing
spec:
  host: pricing.shop.svc.cluster.local
  subsets:
    - name: v1
      labels: { version: v1 }
    - name: v2
      labels: { version: v2 }
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: pricing
spec:
  hosts: [pricing.shop.svc.cluster.local]
  http:
    - timeout: 2s
      retries:
        attempts: 2
        perTryTimeout: 500ms
        retryOn: connect-failure,refused-stream,unavailable,503
      route:
        - destination: { host: pricing.shop.svc.cluster.local, subset: v1 }
          weight: 95
        - destination: { host: pricing.shop.svc.cluster.local, subset: v2 }
          weight: 5
code.note: The overall timeout (2 s) caps all retries together, and perTryTimeout keeps one slow attempt from eating the budget. Moving the canary is a one-line weight change, no redeploy.

qs.s: Requests flow gateway → A → B → C. The mesh is set to make up to 3 attempts at every hop. C goes down hard. How many requests can reach C for a single user request?
qs.e: Each layer multiplies: the gateway tries A 3 times, each A attempt tries B 3 times, each B attempt tries C 3 times: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. This is how retries turn a slow service into an outage. Retry at one layer, with a budget.

qs.s: You switch a namespace to STRICT mTLS. Immediately, Prometheus scrapes and an old VM-based client fail with connection reset by peer. Why?
o: Envoy crashed after the config change
The workload certificates expired
Cluster DNS cannot resolve the services any more
Clients outside the mesh send plaintext, and STRICT accepts only mTLS; use PERMISSIVE until every client is in the mesh
qs.e: STRICT means every inbound connection must be mTLS from a mesh identity. Expired certificates would break mesh-to-mesh traffic too, not only the outside clients. Migrate with PERMISSIVE first.

qs.s: After Istio sidecar injection, nightly CronJob pods never finish: the app container exits 0, but the pod stays Running. Best fix?
o: The sidecar proxy keeps running; use native sidecars (init containers with restartPolicy: Always) or make the proxy exit when the job is done
Raise the Job's backoffLimit
mTLS blocks the completion signal to the API server; disable mTLS for Jobs
Set activeDeadlineSeconds so Kubernetes kills the pod
qs.e: A pod completes only when all its regular containers exit. Native sidecars are stopped automatically after the main containers finish. A deadline would kill the pod and mark the Job as failed, not succeeded.

qs.s: The pricing service's p99 latency is 1.4 s. This VirtualService is applied. What do callers see for requests that would take longer than 1 s?

code.title: virtualservice.yaml
code.src:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: pricing
spec:
  hosts: [pricing]
  http:
    - timeout: 1s
      retries:
        attempts: 3
        perTryTimeout: 1s
      route:
        - destination: { host: pricing }

o: Up to 3 attempts of 1 s each, so callers wait up to 3 s and usually get an answer
The retries are ignored because retryOn is missing
Slow requests fail with 504 after 1 s: the route timeout caps all attempts together, and it equals the per-try timeout, so there is never time for a retry
The request waits the full 1.4 s, because timeouts apply only to new connections
qs.e: In Istio, the route timeout is the total time for the request, including retries. With timeout = perTryTimeout = 1s, the first attempt uses all of it. attempts counts retries after the first try, so to leave room for every retry: timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout; and per-try timeouts should sit above the service's normal p99. When retryOn is not set, Istio uses its default conditions, so retries are not ignored.

qs.s: Checkout gets bursts of 503 errors from pricing, but pricing's own metrics show no errors and low load. Read the config and the caller's sidecar log. What is happening?

code.title: destinationrule.yaml + sidecar log
code.src:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: pricing
spec:
  host: pricing
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 1
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 1
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 2
# checkout sidecar access log (trimmed):
# "GET /v1/price HTTP/1.1" 503 UO ... "pricing.shop.svc.cluster.local"

o: Pricing is returning 503 under load and its metrics are wrong
The circuit-breaker limits are tiny, so checkout's own Envoy rejects requests locally (flag UO = upstream overflow); pricing never sees them. Raise the pool limits based on real concurrency
mTLS certificates expired between checkout and pricing
Pricing has no healthy endpoints
qs.e: UO means the client-side proxy refused the request because the connection pool or pending queue was full. That is why the server sees nothing. No healthy endpoints would show UH, and certificate problems would show TLS or connection errors. Circuit-breaker settings must be sized from measured concurrency, not copied from examples.

qs.s: Checkout calls pricing with an HTTP client that makes up to 3 attempts. Both run with Istio sidecars, and there is no VirtualService for pricing. Pricing goes down hard (connections refused). How many connection attempts can reach pricing for one checkout call?
qs.e: Istio's default retry policy retries twice (3 attempts) on connection failures, even with no VirtualService. Each of the 3 app attempts becomes up to 3 proxy attempts: 3 × 3 = 9. Many teams do not know the default exists. Decide on one retry layer and turn the other off (or set mesh retries to 0 for that route).

qs.s: A cluster has 2,000 pods. All need mTLS between services; only about 5 services need HTTP features like canary traffic splits. The team is choosing between Istio sidecar mode and ambient mode. Which choice best fits?
o: Ambient mode: ztunnel on each node gives mTLS to every pod without a proxy per pod, and waypoint proxies are added only for the few services that need HTTP routing
Sidecar mode everywhere, because ambient mode cannot do mTLS
No mesh: use Kubernetes NetworkPolicies, which encrypt traffic
Sidecar mode only for the 5 services, and no mTLS for the rest
qs.e: Ambient mode separates L4 (mTLS, identity) from L7 (HTTP routing). That removes 2,000 sidecars and their CPU and memory, and avoids sidecar start-up and Job problems. NetworkPolicies control which pods may connect, but they do not encrypt. Leaving most services without mTLS fails the main requirement.

interview.q: A team asks whether to introduce a service mesh. How do you decide?
answer: Start from the problem: required service-to-service mTLS and identity (compliance, zero trust), consistent traffic policy across many languages, or canary traffic splitting. If none of these is real, do not adopt one.
Count the cost: proxies use CPU and memory (Istio docs: about 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB per Envoy sidecar at 1,000 rps), add a little latency per hop, and need upgrades by a platform team.
Alternatives: libraries for timeouts and retries, OpenTelemetry for metrics and traces, NetworkPolicies for access control, cert-manager for TLS where needed.
If yes: choose sidecar vs ambient on purpose, roll out namespace by namespace, start mTLS in PERMISSIVE, and define who owns mesh config.
Set success criteria up front (for example: all east-west traffic mTLS, per-route golden signals) so you can tell if it paid off.
followups: Linkerd or Istio: what would make you choose one?
How would you roll back a mesh adoption?

interview.q: How does mesh mTLS give each service an identity, and what does it not protect you from?
answer: The mesh control plane acts as a certificate authority and issues short-lived certificates bound to the workload's ServiceAccount (a SPIFFE ID such as spiffe://cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/checkout), and rotates them automatically.
Both proxies verify each other, so traffic is encrypted and each side knows which workload is calling. Authorization policies can then say “only checkout may call payments”.
It does not replace application authorization: knowing the caller is checkout does not say which end user is allowed to see which order.
A compromised pod can use its own identity, so least-privilege policies per ServiceAccount matter. Shared ServiceAccounts weaken identity.
It does not cover traffic leaving the mesh (egress) or clients outside it unless you add gateways and policies for them.
followups: What happens if the mesh CA is unavailable for an hour?
How do you migrate to STRICT mTLS without an outage?

interview.q: How do you configure retries in a mesh so they help and do not cause outages?
answer: Retry at one layer only. Know the defaults: Istio already retries twice; app clients and gateways may retry too, and layers multiply.
Retry only safe cases: connection failures, refused streams, 503 from an overloaded instance; and only idempotent requests (GET, or POST with an idempotency key).
Set perTryTimeout above the service's normal p99 and the total timeout large enough to allow the retries you configured.
Limit retry volume: few attempts, and retry budgets or circuit breakers (outlier detection, connection pools) so a sick service gets less traffic, not more.
Watch retry rates and UO/UH response flags; a rise in retries is an early warning before user-facing errors.
followups: Why is retrying a POST dangerous without idempotency keys?
How do retries interact with a canary at 5%?
